September 23, 2026

Ms. Debbie-Anne A. Reese, Secretary
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
888 First Street, N.E.
Washington, D.C. 20426

Re:       Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC
          FERC Docket No. PF26-9-000
          Desert Southwest Expansion Project
          Draft Environmental Resource Reports 4, 6 and 7, and Appendix 1G

Dear Ms. Reese:

On March 27, 2026, in compliance with the requirements of 18 Code of Federal Regulations ("C.F.R.")
§157.21(b) 1, Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC ("Transwestern") requested that the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission ("FERC" or "Commission") begin its review of the proposed Desert Southwest
Expansion Project ("Project") using FERC's Pre-Filing Review Process ("Pre-Filing"), and FERC assigned
Docket No. PF26-9-000 to the Project. On April 3, 2026, FERC approved Transwestern's request.

Consistent with Section 157.21(f)(10) 2 of the Commission's pre-filing procedures, Transwestern is filing
draft Environmental Resource Reports 4, 6 and 7, and Appendix 1G of Draft Resource Report 1 for the
Project. Transwestern will include final Resource Reports 4, 6 and 7 and Appendix 1G as part of the final
Environmental Report as Exhibit F-1 to the certificate application, which is anticipated to be filed by
November 30, 2026.

Transwestern respectfully requests that the information submitted as Public be placed on the internet as
“Public Information, and the Privileged information submitted as “CUI/Privileged Information – Do Not
Release” be accorded special treatment pursuant to 18 CFR § 388.112.

This filing is being submitted electronically to the Commission’s eFiling website pursuant to the
Commission’s Order No. 703, Filing via the Internet Guidelines, issued on November 15, 2007, in FERC
Docket No. RM07-16-000. Any questions or comments regarding this filing should be directed to the
undersigned at (713) 989-2605.

Respectfully submitted,


  /s/ Blair Lichtenwalter
__________________________
Blair Lichtenwalter, Sr. Director

1.0     INTRODUCTION

This Erosion Control and Revegetation Plan (ECRP) outlines the procedures that Transwestern Pipeline
Company, LLC (Transwestern) will utilize during construction of the Desert Southwest Expansion Project
(Project) to minimize erosion, sedimentation, and enhance revegetation success on all lands affected by the
Project. The goal of this ECRP is to identify and specify the Best Management Practices (BMPs) that will
be utilized to protect soil productivity and water quality by controlling soil erosion, soil displacement, and
the loss of surface organic matter. The ECRP also describes the measures that will be implemented to
minimize impacts from potential soil compaction. The revegetation measures have been prescribed to
stabilize disturbed areas and to revegetate the rights-of-way to support the preconstruction land use (i.e.,
rangelands, croplands, hayfields and pasturelands) as quickly as possible following construction.
Additionally, measures have been designed to mitigate impacts to wildlife habitat.

The erosion control and revegetation procedures were developed using the Federal Energy Regulatory
Commission’s (FERC’s) Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and Maintenance Plan (Plan) and Wetland
and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures (Procedures) which have been modified by
Transwestern to more appropriately fit the desert Southwest environment crossed by the Project through
west Texas, southwest New Mexico, and eastern Arizona. The modified Plan and Procedures are referred
to as Transwestern’s FERC Plan and Transwestern’s FERC Procedures and are provided in Attachments A
and B. The ECRP incorporates BMPs provided by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and erosion
control and revegetation guidelines provided by the Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) and
various Soil and Water Conservation Districts.

2.0     PROJECT DESCRIPTION

This expansion Project includes a 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline and lateral pipelines as well as new
compressor stations (CS), associated meter and regulator (M&R) stations, and other aboveground facilities
located in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The permanent aboveground fenced facilities will be located
within Transwestern’s permanent operational right-of-way or land purchased in fee and will be stabilized
by gravel; therefore, these facilities will not be discussed further. The measures in this Plan will be
implemented during construction and maintenance of temporary and permanent access roads and
improvements of existing access roads. Detailed topographic maps (U.S. Geological Survey [USGS] 7.5-
minute topographic quadrangles) of the Project and photo-based alignment sheets are included as
appendices to Resource Report 1.

3.0     EXISTING SITE CONDITIONS

3.1     Topographic Setting

A summary of the Project’s topographic setting for the mainline is provided in this section, and a detailed
description can be found in Resource Report 6. Between milepost (MP) 0 and approximately MP 45, the
mainline traverses the Pecos Valley section of the Great Plains Physiographic Province in western Texas.
Terrain is predominantly level to gently undulating and consists of broad alluvial and eolian surfaces with
shallow swales, low ridges, localized dune fields, and intermittent drainageways.

From approximately MP 45 to MP 214, the mainline crosses the Sacramento section of the Basin and Range
Physiographic Province through Trans-Pecos Texas and into southern New Mexico. This segment contains
greater topographic variation along the route and includes bedrock ranges, dissected uplands, plateaus,
broad intermontane basins, and extensive piedmont surfaces. Slopes are generally gentle on distal alluvial



DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                     1                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                        DRAFT                                           ECRP



fans and basin floors but become moderate to steep near mountain fronts, canyon mouths, escarpments, and
bedrock ridges.

Between approximately MP 214 and MP 470, the mainline traverses the Mexican Highland section of the
Basin and Range Physiographic Province across southern New Mexico and southeastern Arizona. The
landscape consists of broad structural and alluvial basins separated by isolated mountain ranges and bedrock
uplands. Basin interiors support extended areas of nearly level to gently sloping terrain, while localized
moderate to steep relief occurs at mountain fronts, bedrock projections, and interbasin divides.

From approximately MP 470 to the western terminus near MP 525, the mainline crosses the Sonoran Desert
section of the Basin and Range Physiographic Province in south-central Arizona. The terrain generally
becomes lower and more open toward the west, although isolated mountain fronts and bedrock hills produce
localized areas of moderate relief.

Appendix 7B to Resource Report 7 provides the landscape position of each of the soil mapping units crossed
by the Project with elevation ranges.

3.2       Climate

The project area is characterized by hot summers (95 to 105oF) and mild winters, with high
evapotranspiration rates. Average rainfall ranges between 7 to 13 inches. Higher elevation areas along the
Project may receive more precipitation, and lower elevations, such as along the Mojave Energy Park
Lateral, may receive less precipitation. More than half of the annual rainfall occurs during the monsoon
season between mid-June through September, with the wettest period typically occurring between mid-July
and August (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration [NOAA] 2026 and Western Regional
Climate Center 2025).

4.0       PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION ACTIVITIES

The Project will be designed, constructed, tested, operated, and maintained to conform with U.S.
Department of Transportation (DOT) requirements, 49 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 192;
FERC’s regulations, 18 CFR §380.15; Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA)
regulations; and other applicable federal and state regulations. In addition to the DOT requirements,
Transwestern will construct and restore disturbed areas in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Plan and
Procedures (see Attachments A and B).

4.1       Pipeline Routing and Design

To minimize overall adverse impacts, Transwestern co-located the mainline with existing infrastructure for
more than 80 percent of the route. The laterals have also been co-located with existing infrastructure where
feasible. Design efforts to maximize co-location with existing infrastructure follows the principles of
Section 503 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) utilizing existing corridors to the
extent practical to minimize adverse environmental impacts and a proliferation of separate rights-of-way.

The Project was designed based on construction feasibility and safety and reliability factors associated with
maintaining and operating a large-diameter high pressure natural gas pipeline. As described in Resource
Report 10, other important routing criteria were also considered, including:

      •   avoiding residential areas and structures;
      •   avoiding sensitive or protected areas;
      •   avoiding Tribal lands;


DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                       2                TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                      DRAFT                                               ECRP



      •   minimizing impacts to cultural resources, where feasible;
      •   avoiding state and federal parks and monuments;
      •   accommodating landowner requests (e.g., routing on edges of parcels and agricultural fields);
      •   when co-locating, prioritizing a single side of existing infrastructure to minimize crossings and to
          maintain a consistent working side that facilitates construction;
      •   minimizing the number of existing infrastructure crossings (e.g., foreign pipelines, roads, canals,
          and railroads);
      •   minimizing side slope and steep slope construction; and
      •   considering construction requirements necessary for a 48-inch diameter mainline and the various
          diameter laterals.

4.2       Construction Schedule

Construction of the mainline is expected to be completed in 20 months beginning in April 2028 with
completion in November 2029. The lateral construction varies but typically would be complete in less than
6 months.

4.3       Pipeline Construction Sequence

Transwestern will use multiple construction spreads to efficiently construct the mainline. Lateral
construction will likely be limited to single spreads. Within each mainline spread, the construction sequence
will typically proceed systematically as follows:

      •   preconstruction survey, marking and staking;
      •   access road improvement;
      •   vegetation clearing and grading;
      •   installation of erosion control BMPs;
      •   topsoiling (where required);
      •   trenching;
      •   pipe stringing;
      •   welding and coating pipe;
      •   lowering pipe and backfilling;
      •   strength (hydrostatic) testing; and
      •   clean-up and restoration.

The construction activities for each spread will generally occur in sequence or in assembly-line fashion
along the right-of-way with one crew following the next from clearing until final cleanup. Each spread is
planned to encompass all construction activities within a specific milepost range (see Table 4.3-1). Using
multiple construction spreads is a BMP that will minimize the time necessary to complete construction
reducing the time of disturbance.

4.3.1   Preconstruction Survey
Prior to construction, the construction right-of-way limits, including the boundaries of ATWS shown on
the alignment sheets, will be clearly marked/staked. Environmental Inspectors (EIs) will verify the limits
of the staked construction areas. Consistent with Section IV.A.1 of Transwestern’s FERC Plan,
Transwestern will limit disturbance to those areas shown on the alignment sheets and approved through a
Notice to Proceed from FERC. No disturbance will be allowed to occur outside of these areas without
appropriate surveys (cultural, threatened and endangered species, residential, etc.), other federal, state, or
local permits and prior written approval from FERC.

Access roads, overhead utilities, and buried utilities will be located, marked, and signed to prevent
accidental damage during pipeline construction. Sensitive areas to be protected from disturbance will be
marked with t-posts and brightly colored rope, flagging, or construction fence so as to be visible to
equipment operators. These areas will also be located on the alignment sheets issued for construction and
presented during preconstruction environmental training. Equipment will only be allowed to enter and
operate within the delineated limits of disturbance, access roads, etc. Flagging, signs, and other markings
identifying the limits of disturbance will be maintained through all phases of construction and will be
routinely checked by the EIs.

Mainline construction will primarily use a 150-foot-wide construction right-of-way with ATWS where
necessary. The construction rights-of-way for the proposed laterals vary between 75 feet and 100 feet in
width depending on the diameter of the lateral pipeline. In specified areas, such as sensitive areas or
residential areas, the construction rights-of-way have been reduced to minimize disturbance. ATWS have
been located at least 50 feet from the edge of dry washes, where feasible, based on topographic conditions
or other existing constraints. As outlined in Transwestern’s FERC Procedures (V.B.2.a.), the ATWS may
be shifted to within 10 feet of the top bank of the dry wash crossings during construction when no water is
present.

4.3.2   Vegetation Clearing and Grading
The flagged limits of disturbance will be maintained throughout all construction phases and will be
monitored by Transwestern’s EIs so all activities are restricted to certificated limits. Grading the
construction right-of-way in upland areas will be limited to the minimum required to provide a safe working
area necessary to construct the pipeline. Where necessary, vegetation clearing will be completed by
mowing, mulching, or scalping off the tops of the shrubs with a brushhog, hydro ax, or a bulldozer. The
salvaged vegetative material will provide a source of seed and vegetative propagules (i.e., roots, rhizomes,
stolons, etc.) to improve revegetation success. The surface soil, desert pavement, and cleared vegetation
material will be left in-place, on the non-working side of the right-of-way (topsoil and spoil storage areas),
where grading is not required to create a safe working plane. The mowed/mulched vegetation material will
provide a vegetative/organic marker for operators during backfilling and regrading operations. It will
indicate that they have reached the original ground surface during backfilling and surface soil spreading to
minimize disturbance to the undisturbed soils on the non-working side of the right-of-way. The EI, Chief
Inspector, or Transwestern’s Representative will determine areas where it is not feasible to salvage
rangeland surface soil based on topographic conditions, available workspace, and bedrock or surface rock
conditions. The salvaged vegetation and topsoil materials may be stored on the working and/or non-
working side of the construction right-of-way to minimize movement of topsoil during grading and
restoration activities as determined during construction. Where it is not feasible to salvage rangeland
surface soil, Transwestern will report the locations by MP and provide the rationale to FERC in weekly or
bi-weekly reports.

To minimize disturbance to desert rangelands, Transwestern is not proposing additional ATWS to store the
salvaged vegetative and surface soils materials but, instead, proposes to store this material within the


DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                     4                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                      DRAFT                                                ECRP



construction right-of-way. In rugged topographic areas, excavated spoil material may be placed abutting
and potentially on top of the salvaged vegetation/surface soils to minimize the need for ATWS. The
grading/excavating/restoring sequence will be a first out/last in approach. This means the soil first
excavated will be the last material redistributed across the right-of-way to preserve the surface soil and soil
seed bank. It is Transwestern’s opinion that creating additional disturbance (i.e., ATWS) in desert habitats
to separate the salvaged surface materials from the spoil is not beneficial and would create more long-term
disturbance impacts.

Where topographic conditions allow and where grading is not required on the non-working side of the right-
of-way, vegetation clearing (by mowing, brush hogging or other methods) that leave root systems intact,
will allow sprouting species to reestablish from existing root systems which will enhance revegetation. The
existing root systems may include fourwing saltbush, brittlebush, acacia, creosote bush, mesquite and Palo
Verde. During clearing operations, at dry wash crossings where woody shrub vegetation is dense, and the
cleared vegetative material cannot be readily incorporated into the surface soil, the EI will determine where
the cleared vegetation can be salvaged and stored on the edge of the construction right-of-way so that this
vegetation debris can be respread as surface mulch after restoration on the wash banks to provide cover for
small mammals and reptiles along these movement corridors until vegetation is re-established.

In Arizona, Transwestern will appropriately permit and conduct land clearing according to the Arizona
Department of Agriculture Native Plants Administrative Code rules (see Article 11). During clearing
operations, where feasible based on topographic conditions and available workspace, Arizona protected
native plant species will be avoided along the edges of the construction rights-of-way. Clearing and grading
activities will follow the procedures outlined in the Noxious Weed and Invasive Plant Management Plan in
Attachment E.

4.3.3   Installation of Erosion Control BMPs
Section 5.1 details the temporary erosion control measures Transwestern will implement and maintain until
successful revegetation has been achieved.

4.3.4   Topsoiling
Topsoil segregation will be performed over the trenchline and subsoil storage area in croplands, hayfields,
pastures, and residential areas. Transwestern will stockpile topsoil from the trenchline and subsoil storage
area separately from all subsoil and will replace the two horizons in the proper order during backfilling and
final grading. Topsoil segregation will be performed in these areas to prevent mixing of the soil horizons
to prevent the potential loss of soil fertility or incorporation of excess rock into the topsoil. Implementation
of proper topsoil segregation will help to ensure post-construction crop productivity and revegetation
success. Agricultural areas where topsoil will be segregated are identified in Resource Report 7 in Table
7.3-2 and will be shown on the alignment sheets.

4.3.5   Trenching
The depth of the trench will be sufficient to provide a minimum depth of cover of 30 inches in normal soil,
18 inches in consolidated rock, and at least 48 inches in agricultural lands. Transwestern will strive to
exceed these minimum DOT requirements provided in 49 CFR Part192 where feasible and will achieve 36
inches of cover in Class I locations with normal soil and up to 24 inches of cover in consolidated rock areas.

Road and railroad crossings will follow DOT regulations. As described in Resource Report 6, the pipeline
cover depth at dry wash crossings will be based on the scour analysis to reduce the risk of future pipeline
exposure resulting from scour, migration, and flooding processes at surveyed waterbody crossings.




DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                      5                   TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                     DRAFT                                               ECRP



4.3.6   Pipe Installation
After trenching is complete, the pipe sections will be strung along the trench, bent to fit the contour of the
trench bottom, aligned, welded together, and placed on temporary supports along the edge of the trench.
All welds will be visually inspected, non-destructively tested (using radiographic or equivalent methods),
and repaired, if necessary. Line pipe, normally mill-coated prior to stringing, will require field applied
coating at the welded joints prior to final inspection. The entire pipeline coating will be inspected and
tested to locate and repair flaws and voids. The pipe assembly will then be lowered into the trench by side-
boom tractors and excavators.

4.3.7   Backfilling
The trench will be backfilled using a backfilling machine or bladed equipment. No foreign substance,
including skids, welding rods, containers, brush, or refuse of any kind, will be permitted in the backfill.
Segregated topsoil will not be used for padding the pipe,

Trench plugs/breakers will be installed in the trench on slopes prior to backfilling to prevent water from
flowing along the pipeline and eroding trench backfill materials. During the monsoon season, temporary
trench plugs will be installed at all waterbody/dry wash crossings, as necessary, to prevent diversion of
water into upland portions of the pipeline trench and to keep accumulated trench water out of the waterbody
or dry wash (Transwestern’s FERC Procedures V.6.10.c.). However, Transwestern will backfill the trench
as quickly as possible to avoid the need to install temporary trench plugs/breakers. Trench plugs/breakers
are described in detail in Section 5.2.1.

The contractor will backfill and stabilize areas as soon as possible according to Transwestern’s FERC Plan
(Section V.A.1.) which specifies that final grading topsoil replacement and installation of permanent
erosion control structures will be completed within 35 days after backfilling the trench (10 days in
residential areas). However, if seasonal or other weather causes delays, temporary erosion control measures
(temporary slope breakers and sediment barriers) will be maintained until conditions allow completion of
cleanup.

4.3.8   Hydrostatic Testing
After backfilling, the mainline and laterals will be strength tested in accordance with DOT regulations to
ensure that the system is capable of operating at the maximum operating pressure. Should a leak or break
occur, the line would be repaired and retested until the specifications are achieved. Water for hydrostatic
testing will be purchased from commercial or municipal sources or from groundwater sources. If water for
hydrostatic testing is acquired from groundwater wells, Transwestern will obtain all necessary
appropriations and withdrawal permits (see Section 9.0 for hydrostatic testing and dewatering details).

4.3.9   Restoration
After the mainline and laterals have been backfilled and tested, disturbed areas will be restored, as nearly
as possible, to their original contours. Permanent erosion control measures will be installed and
revegetation will occur as discussed below.

5.0     BEST MANAGEMENT PRACTICES

This ECRP will be used by contractors as a primary reference during construction on all lands crossed by
the mainline and laterals. This ECRP provides guidelines for installing temporary and permanent BMPs to
prevent or minimize erosion and offsite sedimentation and to protect sensitive resources and water quality.
Attachment C provides typical BMPs that may be used during construction. BMP materials will be stored
at designated yards or staging areas along the construction right-of-way.


DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                     6                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                     DRAFT                                                  ECRP



In accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see Attachment A.), Transwestern will employ a lead EI
and multiple EIs per spread for each of the pipeline spreads listed in Table 4.3-1. The lead EIs will be
responsible for agency notifications and reporting requirements within each construction spread and will
have oversight and ultimate authority over assistant EIs. The lead EIs will conduct routine meetings and
maintain communications to uphold consistency and compliance with the appropriate federal, state, and
local regulations and permit requirements. All EIs will be onsite during active construction and will have
peer status with all other activity inspectors. The EIs will have authority to stop activities that violate the
measures set forth in this ECRP as well as other permits and authorizations and will have the authority to
order corrective action. Transwestern will adequately staff additional EIs on each spread depending on the
length and complexity of each spread. At a minimum, each EI will be responsible for:

  •   Ensuring compliance with the measures set forth in this ECRP, the requirements of Transwestern’s
      FERC Plan and Procedures, and all other environmental permits and approvals, as well as
      environmental requirements in landowner agreements, including the federal right-of-way grant;

  •   Identifying, documenting, and overseeing corrective actions, as necessary, to bring an activity back
      into compliance;

  •   Verifying that the limits of authorized construction work areas and locations of access roads are
      properly marked before clearing;

  •   Verifying the location of signs and highly visible flagging marking the boundaries of sensitive
      resource areas, dry wash crossings, or areas with special requirements along the construction work
      area;

  •   Identifying erosion/sediment control and stabilization needs in all areas;

  •   Locating dewatering structures and slope breakers to ensure they will not direct water into known

5.1.5    Wind Erosion and Dust Control
Wind erosion occurs when dry, sandy or fine-grained, non-cohesive surface soils are exposed and
transported by wind. The strongest prevailing winds in the project area primarily occur in the spring (March
- April) and during the July-August monsoon season when gust fronts (haboob) can occur (NOAA 2026b
and Arizona State University [ASU] 2026). Under field conditions, soil begins to move when the wind
velocity reaches about 13 miles per hour (mph) at one foot above the ground surface (NRCS undated).
Although the average monthly wind speeds are less than 13 mph across the project area, the average
monthly peak wind gust ranges exceed 13 mph in all months and range between 21 mph near Willcox in
December to about 33 mph in April near Deming. Single-event extreme weather occurrences (such as
monsoon severe thunderstorms or strong winter cold fronts) can produce localized wind gusts that
significantly exceed the multi-year averages (NOAA 2026b). Therefore, wind erosion across disturbed
areas can be expected in all months in the project area.

Additionally, fugitive dust is likely an issue during the entire year based on the arid climate. To minimize
wind erosion and fugitive dust during construction, Transwestern will implement the Fugitive Dust Control
Plan (see Appendix 9D to Resource Report 9), which includes the following BMPs:

   •    disturb no more earth than required for construction to occur;
   •    water the construction right-of-way, laydown areas, and temporary access roads at least daily in
        areas of active construction near residential areas, if necessary, as determined by the EI;
   •    apply tackifier or dust control products (if approved) to minimize water use;
   •    control construction-related traffic speeds on dirt access roads and on linear facility rights-of-way;
   •    adhere to speeds as determined by the property owner on private lands and by the county or federal
        land management agency on public roads;

        control fugitive dust;
   •    ensure that speeds on the construction right-of-way will not exceed 15 mph where fugitive dust
        can be generated;
   •    decrease speed limits when excessive winds prevail and where sensitive areas such as residences
        or public roads may be adjacent to access roads or the construction right-of-way;
   •    maintain speed limit signs for the duration of the construction, and place signs where access roads
        intersect the construction right-of-way. Signs will be designed to endure weather conditions and

   •    water temporarily stockpiled soils to create a semi-hard protective layer/crust to minimize wind

When applying water for dust control, water trucks will spray only enough water to control the dust or to
reach the optimum soil moisture content to create a surface crust. Runoff should not be generated during

5.2.3   Soil Compaction
Resource Report 7 describes the potential for the Project to cause soil compaction during clearing and
construction activities. Soil compaction and rutting are greatly affected by soil moisture content, and the
arid climate of the project area minimizes the periods when soils are wet. Most soils are susceptible to
compaction from repeated heavy equipment traffic which will occur on the working side of the construction
right-of-way. During restoration, surfaces compacted from construction activities will be relieved or
mitigated by typical regrading, recontouring, scarifying, and final cleanup activities. Mitigating
compaction will promote infiltration, reduce surface water runoff, minimize erosion, and enhance
revegetation efforts. Scarification will occur prior to topsoil or surface soil redistribution.

Transwestern will test for soil compaction in agricultural areas (e.g., active croplands, hayfields, and
pastures), residential areas. Soil compaction testing (using a penetrometer or similar device) will be
conducted on the same soil type under similar moisture and surface conditions as specified in Section V.C.1
of Transwestern’s FERC Plan. Pursuant to Section II.B.8 of Transwestern’s FERC Plan, the EI will be
responsible for conducting soil compaction testing and determining corrective measures, including
localized deep scarification or ripping to an average depth of up to 18 inches (where feasible) utilizing
appropriate rippers, including wing-tipped rippers or a Paraplow along all areas of the construction right-
of-way. The EI will also verify that appropriate scarification methods are used in areas of shallow soil (i.e.,
shallow to weather bedrock, restrictive layers such as caliche or petrocalcic layers) so that scarification does
not occur to a depth that could hinder restoration efforts by generating additional surface coarse fragments
or mixing rooting zone soils with rubble, poor water holding, or low fertility materials.

The trench line does not receive repeated heavy equipment traffic like the working side of the right-of-way,
consequently the potential for compaction to occur over the trench line is limited. Furthermore, the trench
is backfilled with excavated trench material toward the end of construction activities, just before restoration.
Backfilling is the next to last step in the construction sequence which would limit traffic and the potential
for compaction to occur over the backfilled trench.

These measures will ensure that compaction is mitigated; that long-term impacts to soil productivity do not
occur; and that the potential for increases in surface water runoff, soil erosion, and sediment delivery is
minimized.

6.0     WATERBODY/DRY WASH CROSSINGS

Only two perennial waterbodies are crossed by the Project (both in Texas: Pecos River/MP 31.33 and Salt
Creek/MP 43.74). To minimize waterbody/dry wash impacts and riparian fragmentation, Transwestern has
routed the Project to be co-located with existing pipelines and has abutted existing easements where
feasible.

Except for the two perennial waterbodies, the Central Arizona Project (CAP), and several canals (man-
made features with artificial perennial flow) in Arizona, all other waterbodies crossed by the Project are
classified as intermittent or ephemeral dry washes or man-made ditches/canals. Trenchless crossing
methods (horizontal directional drill [HDD], direct pipe, or conventional bore) will be used to cross the
Pecos River, Salt Creek, CAP and several canals in Arizona, as well as the Rio Grande and San Pedro
rivers, which are intermittent waterbodies. Other irrigation canals and ditches not crossed by trenchless
crossing methods (HDD or bore) will be crossed according to the irrigation district or landowner
specifications. Transwestern developed a Horizonal Directional Drill Monitoring, Inadvertent Return
Response, and Contingency Plan (see Appendix 2G to Resource Report 2) to minimize the potential for
inadvertent release of drilling fluids and associated impacts.

The surveyed ephemeral or intermittent open water features include 24 man-made stock ponds and 13
playas. Waterbody features dry at the time of construction will be crossed using typical cross-country
construction methods as described in Transwestern’s FERC Procedures (see Section V.B.3.g. in Attachment
B) using standard upland construction techniques in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Plan.

Average rainfall across the Project ranges between 7 and 13 inches. Over half of the annual rainfall occurs
during the monsoon season from mid-June through September with the wettest period typically occurring
between mid-July through August. Rain events typically occur as short duration high intensity thunder
showers that may result in runoff and flash flooding.

To minimize the potential for construction across dry washes occurring during runoff/flash flooding events,
Transwestern’s EIs, Company Representative, and construction contractor will monitor upcoming weather
forecasts to determine if significant rainfall is anticipated at times when construction across dry washes is
planned (between initial disturbance and final stabilization of the feature). To the extent practical,
Transwestern will avoid construction across dry washes during periods of anticipated rainfall. If rainfall is
not expected to be significant (e.g., less than 0.5 inch) and Transwestern determines that construction should
proceed, environmental crews would be notified of the location of planned crossings and would be available
to respond quickly if additional erosion control devices are required. If flow conditions develop during
construction of a given dry wash crossing, Transwestern’s EIs and environmental crews would be notified
immediately to determine the extent of the flow and would install additional erosion control devices as
necessary. If flows are significant, and siltation is likely to occur, work would be stopped until flows have
ceased or have decreased to the point where potential erosion can be contained within the construction work
area. If severe monsoon storm events are forecast in an area during the scheduled crossings, as determined
by the EI and Transwestern’s Representative, construction across the waterbody feature would not be
conducted until flow/weather conditions allow, as approved by the EI and Transwestern’s Representative.

If a dry wash is flowing at the time of construction, and Transwestern determines based on construction
timing, schedules, or other conditions, that it is not feasible to pause construction until there is no perceptible
flow, Transwestern would utilize dry crossing methods (flume or dam and pump) consistent with the
requirements of federal, state, and local agencies with specific authority to regulate the waterbody crossing.

construction, Transwestern will implement the procedures outlined in the SPAR Plan.

6.2     Material Delivery and Storage

Transwestern will use various contractor yards for material delivery and storage. Materials will be brought
onto the right-of-way as they are needed and will be stored away from waterbodies and wetlands.
Secondary containment will be provided for fuel, lubricating oils, and other potential contaminating liquids.

7.0     WETLAND CROSSINGS

The Project will only cross two wetlands, and they are associated with the two perennial waterbodies (Pecos
River/MP 31.33 and Salt Creek/MP 43.74). To avoid impacts, the Pecos River and Salt Creek and their
associated wetlands will be crossed by HDD. No other wetlands were delineated that would be impacted
by the construction rights-of-way.

8.0     MAINTENANCE AND PERIODIC EVALUATION

Erosion control structures will be maintained in accordance with Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see
Attachment A). The EI will inspect temporary erosion control structures at least daily in areas of active
construction. In areas where active construction is not occurring, inspections will be made at least weekly.
All structures will be inspected by the EI within 24 hours of 0.5 inch or greater of rainfall or as required by
state and local jurisdictions. Whenever possible, the EI will evaluate erosion control measures prior to a
predicted storm event and implement measures needed to prevent off right-of-way sedimentation.
Inspections will be documented and available for agency review upon request.

The EI will be responsible for ensuring that ineffective temporary erosion control measures are repaired
within 24 hours of discovery. If poor weather conditions prevail, the EI will notify construction crews
when to initiate precautionary measures. The EI will ensure that the contractor has adequate equipment,
materials, and crews available to respond rapidly to storm events. It is the responsibility of the EI to advise
the Chief Inspector when wet weather or other conditions make it advisable to restrict construction activities
to avoid excessive rutting in sensitive areas (see Section 5.0 for a list of EI responsibilities).

9.0     HYDROSTATIC TEST WATER AND DEWATERING

During the Project’s final design phase, Transwestern will determine the number of required hydrostatic
test sections, which will have varying lengths and water volume requirements (see Resource Report 1).
During the test, it may be necessary to release water at each of the section breaks; however, Transwestern



DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                     16                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                       DRAFT                                                 ECRP



will conserve water as much as practical and minimize release by cascading water between test sections,
where feasible. Additionally, where feasible, water that does need to be released may be stored in tanks or
lined ponds and used for dust control or hydroseeding.

Permission to release the hydrostatic test water will be obtained through the governing agencies and in
compliance with applicable federal or state permits. Release rates would range from several hundred
gallons per minute (gpm) to several thousand gpm. The specific hydrostatic release rate at each dewater
location cannot be estimated at this time because the rate will be dependent on contractor means and
methods in addition to a number of factors specific to each location. These variables include: the volume
of water to be released, completion dates for adjoining test segments, topographic conditions of the
locations, elevation differences between test sections and the direction of flow (uphill/downhill) between
the test section, size of the test head piping, kind and size of the dewater structure, infiltration properties of
the surrounding soils, and location of any sensitive resources or facilities (e.g., roads, residences) in the
vicinity of the dewater locations. The rate would be controlled to prevent scour, erosion, and potential
effects or sediment migration to sensitive resources or facilities. The test water will be released into an
appropriately sized dewatering device such as a straw bale structure to dissipate energy of the test water
flow, filter the test water, and to allow release of the test water as sheet flow back onto the ground or into a
dry wash, as depicted in Figure 14 in Attachment C. Water sourcing and disposal associated with hydrostatic
testing of the compressor stations will be the responsibility of the contractors building the facilities. They
will supply and dispose of water used.

During construction there is a possibility, in the limited areas where high groundwater may be present, that
trench dewatering may be required where access to the trench is necessary to make welds such as tie-in
locations. Based on analysis of NRCS soils data (see Resource Report 7), soils with high water tables (less
than 60 inches) crossed by the mainline are associated with drainages or basin crossings such as near the
Pecos and Rio Grande rivers, Salt Basin in Texas, and Bass and Wildcat canyons in Arizona. The laterals
will not cross any soils with high water tables.

Transwestern’s EIs will visually monitor the release of hydrostatic test water and trench dewatering
activities to ensure that no erosion or sedimentation occurs. In addition, the EIs will ensure that turbid
water is not discharged to waters of the state. If an EI or authorized agency representative determines that
a discharge is occurring from hydrostatic testing or trench dewatering, the receiving water will be visually
monitored for turbidity. If turbidity is observed, the hydrostatic test water release or trench dewatering
operation would be immediately adjusted/reinstalled to ensure that the discharge to surface water is stopped
and water quality standards are not exceeded.

10.0    NON-STORMWATER DEWATERING

The only non-stormwater releases associated with construction are trench and hydrostatic test dewatering.
All water associated with trench dewatering will be pumped to filter bags using the trench dewatering BMPs
outlined on Figures 15 and 16 in Attachment C. Trench dewatering may also occur to a strawbale discharge
structure, similar to Figure 14 in Attachment C, which is designed and appropriately sized for the expected
trench dewatering volume

11.0    RESTORATION AND REVEGETATION

Initial reclamation of disturbed areas will begin as soon as possible after construction. Waterbody crossings
will be stabilized and temporary sediment barriers will be installed within 24 hours of completion of
backfilling in accordance with Section V.C.2 of Transwestern’s FERC Procedures (see Attachment B). On
dry open cut crossings (flume or dam and pump), streambed and streambank stabilization will be completed
before returning flow to the waterbody channel. Final grading and permanent erosion control measures of

upland areas will be completed within 35 days (10 days in residential areas) after the trench is backfilled,
weather and soil conditions permitting, as outlined in Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see Section V.A.1).
During final cleanup and initial reclamation, permanent repairs of fences, gates, drainage ditches, and other
structures removed or damaged during construction will be completed.

Transwestern will work with individual landowners to address restoration of active agricultural areas such
as croplands, hayfields, pastures and orchards, as well as residential lawns, ornamental shrubs, gardens, and
other landscaping, if affected by the Project. In active agricultural areas, Transwestern will encourage the
landowner to complete final restoration efforts in these areas and will compensate the landowner for these
efforts. In residential areas, Transwestern will utilize contractors familiar with local horticultural and lawn
establishment procedures for reclamation work or will compensate the landowner to restore these areas.
Specific reclamation procedures will be determined during negotiations with individual landowners.

11.1    Recontouring

All graded areas associated with construction will be regraded and recontoured, as closely as feasible, to
blend into the surrounding landscape and to reestablish natural drainage patterns. The emphasis during
recontouring will be to return the entire right-of-way to its approximate original contours, to stabilize slopes,
control surface drainage, and to aesthetically blend into the adjacent contours. Ruts and other scars will be
regraded, and all drainage ditches will be returned to their preconstruction conditions. Existing culverts
that are damaged or removed during construction will be replaced to their original or better condition.

11.2    Construction Debris Disposal

During final cleanup, all construction debris (e.g., mats, garbage, drilling fluids) will be cleared from the
right-of-way and disposed of in accordance with state and local regulations. Section 11.6 describes excess
rock removal.

11.3    Soil Compaction

Transwestern will mitigate and test for potential soil compaction as described in Section 5.2.3.

11.4    Scarification

Prior to respreading the topsoil in agricultural areas or surface soils in rangeland areas, the right-of-way
will be scarified, where necessary (as determined by the EI), by disking, ripping, or chiseling to loosen
compacted areas from equipment traffic. Scarifying the subsoil will also promote water infiltration and
improve soil aeration and root penetration. Brush blades, rippers, winged subsoilers, chisel plows,
agricultural disks, or other appropriate equipment may be used to reduce shallow soil compaction.

Scarification will occur in areas where the EI determines that the soil compaction is unacceptable.
Disturbed areas that may require scarification primarily include the work lane and may also include portions
of the passing lane or some ATWS. Scarification will occur on average to a depth of up to 18 inches deep,
where feasible, with rippers spaced not more than 16 inches apart where there is no shallow restrictive layer
(weather bedrock, caliche or petrocalcic layers). Ripping and chisel plowing will also occur when materials
are dry enough to promote shattering of compacted layers.

11.5    Soil Replacement

All salvaged topsoil or surface soil will be uniformly spread over the portions of the right-of-way from
where the soil was salvaged. If compaction occurs during this operation that might not be relieved during


DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                      18                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                      DRAFT                                              ECRP



seedbed preparation, all compacted areas will be scarified. Topsoil spreading will not occur during wet
periods when soils are easily compacted, and all travel over re-topsoiled areas will be restricted.

11.6       Rock Removal

Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see Section V.A.3) requires the removal of excess rock from the top 12 inches
of soil in cultivated or rotated croplands, hayfields, pastures, residential areas, and other areas at the
landowner’s request. In these areas, Transwestern will clean up excess rock to a condition similar to
adjacent portions of the construction right-of-way (e.g., size, density, and distribution). Shallow bedrock is
not expected in agricultural areas; if it is encountered, any excavated rock would be buried only to the top
of the existing bedrock profile. In rangelands or other non-agricultural lands or residential lands, where
shallow bedrock is encountered and rock excavation is required, excess rock will be:

       •   buried in cuts during restoration to reestablish approximate original contours;
       •   redistributed across the right-of-way;
       •   used to block unauthorized access to the right-of-way from access points following construction;
       •   used to create habitat features/rock piles where approved by landowners;
       •   used in erosion control features (i.e., check dams), or
       •   used as rip-rap to stabilize dry wash crossings.

If excess rock requires disposal, it will be considered construction debris, and Transwestern will obtain the
appropriate approvals prior to offsite disposal, unless landowner agreements differ.

11.7       Seedbed Preparation

Seedbed preparation will be conducted, where necessary, immediately prior to seeding to prepare a firm
seedbed conducive to proper seed placement and moisture retention. Seedbed preparation will also be
performed to break up surface crusts and to eliminate weeds which may have developed between initial
reclamation and seeding.

A seedbed will be prepared in disturbed areas, where necessary, using appropriate equipment to provide a
seedbed that is firm, yet rough. A rough seedbed is conducive to capturing or lodging seeds when
broadcasted or hydroseeded, and it reduces runoff and water erosion potential, as well as wind erosion. The
rough seedbed will retain soil moisture for seedling germination and establishment.

In most areas, final right-of-way cleanup procedures are sufficient because they leave a surface smooth
enough to accommodate a drill seeder pulled by a tractor and rough enough to catch broadcasted seed and
trap moisture and runoff. However, additional preparation such as chisel plowing or disking may be
necessary to prepare an adequate seedbed. Surface imprinting, pitting or pocking (small irregular
depressions) may also be completed where determined necessary by the EI or Transwestern’s
Representative, in areas such as steep rugged terrain where drill seeding may not be possible or where
salvage of surface soils is not feasible. Imprinting, pitting, or pocking has been successful in reclamation
of arid lands and mine lands (Shumin Lyn et al. 2026, Abusuwar 1986).

Where residential and cropland areas are disturbed, more intensive ground and seedbed preparations may
be required, including rock collection, grading, and soil preparation/amending. The EI will be responsible
for determining where seedbed preparation measures are required prior to seeding. However, it is
Transwestern’s intent that in cropland areas, through easement agreement negotiations, that the landowner
be compensated to complete final restoration activities.

11.8    Fertilization

Soil amendments are not proposed for use across the Project in arid southwest rangelands because fertilizers
promote weeds that compete with native species (see NRCS ROC in Appendix 7D to Resource Report 7
and Dreesen 2009).

11.9    Seed Mixtures

As required by Transwestern’s FERC Plan, Transwestern has consulted with the NRCS and land
management agencies regarding recommended seed mixtures (see Appendix D to Resource Report 7) and
will continue these consultation efforts. The seed mixtures are under development and are provided in
Attachment D. These initial seed mixtures have been prepared based on the biological surveys (see
Resource Report 3), NRCS SSURGO data and ecological site data (see Resource Report 7), seed vendors
contacts, various seed mixture development tools and native plant databases (Bamert Seed Company 2026,
EcoRestore Portal 2026, Caesar Kleberg Wildlife Research Institute 2026 and Native Plant Society of Texas
2026), and agency recommendations. The species selected in the mixture are native species that are
commercially available. These seed mixtures were developed with the primary intent to stabilize disturbed
areas, control erosion, and inhibit establishment of invasive species. They are based on precipitation ranges
and soil and vegetation types so that disturbed areas are returned to preconstruction land uses as quickly as
possible. Seed mixtures will also be developed for hayfields and pastures crossed by the Project, where
private landowners request that the areas be reseeded. During right-of-way negotiations, private
landowners may also request other seed mixtures than those proposed in Attachment D. Specific landowner
requested seed mixtures will be documented in landowner right-of-way agreements.

The seed mixture seeding rates are based on Pure Live Seed (PLS). All seed will be used within one year
from the testing date. The seed will be free of noxious weeds, and the quantity of total weed seed will be
low or within the limits allowed by Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona seed laws and labeling. The EI will
review all seed tags prior to use to ensure that these procedures are implemented. The seeding rates
specified in Attachment D are based on drilling rates (unless specified otherwise). If broadcast seeding
methods are used, the seeding rate will be doubled. If hydroseeding is used, the broadcast seeding rate will
be used plus any adjustment the hydroseeding company recommends based on equipment specifications.

Transwestern will acquire seed through commercial sources, and if a species is not available, alternative
species, such as those listed in the seed mixture tables will be utilized, or the seeding rates of the other
species in the mixture will be adjusted to account for species that are unavailable. Other native adaptive
species will also be considered and utilized as determined appropriate by the EI or knowledgeable
representative. If alternative species are necessary on federal lands, the alternatives would be approved by
the land management agency prior to use.

11.10 Seeding Timing

Seeding of disturbed areas will occur within six working days of final grading, weather and soil conditions
permitting, consistent with Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see Section V.D.3.d in Attachment A). To enhance
revegetation success, seeding will be targeted to be completed prior to the early onset of monsoon season
in June to mid-July (Dreesen 2009 and NRCS 2018).

11.11 Seeding Methods

Seeding will be conducted using a seed drill, mechanical broadcast seeder, or hydroseeder according to the
guidelines in Transwestern’s FERC Plan. The seed application rates will be as specified for drilling rates
and doubled if using broadcast seeding. Appropriate seed carriers, such as rice hulls, will also be used as


DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                    20                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                     DRAFT                                               ECRP



appropriate based on either drill or broadcast seeding to ensure accurate seeding rates and to help prevent
seed separation. Soil amendments will be applied as indicated in Section 11.8.

Drill Seeding

Drill seeding is the preferred seeding method using an appropriate drill for the location. Rangeland drills
designed for rough terrain and seedbeds (see Section 11.7) are the favored drill seeder. Drills with multiple
seed boxes for varying seed sizes will also be considered when seed mixtures are ordered and bagged
separately. The drills will be accurately calibrated for each seed mixture used to ensure the quantity of seed
applied is as specified for each seed mixture (NRCS 2008).

Broadcast Seeding

Broadcast seeding will be the preferred seeding method on steep or rugged topography or in other areas
that cannot be accessed with drill seeding equipment or areas deemed appropriate for broadcast seeding by
the EI or Transwestern’s Representative. Seed will be broadcast with a mechanical seeder immediately
after the seedbed has been prepared and the soil is loose. This will allow the seeds to be lightly covered as
the soil settles. The area will be lightly dragged with chains or other appropriate harrows to lightly cover
the seed in areas where it is possible, as determined by the EI. Broadcast seeding will occur immediately
prior to application of mulch (straw or wood) or where utilized erosion control fabric is applied.

Hydroseeding

Water sources for hydroseeding will be a consideration in the use of this seeding method, due to the
Project’s remoteness and available water sources. The potential reuse of hydrostatic test water for
hydroseed purposes will be considered based on the locations of hydrostatic test break discharge locations
and available water storage equipment. Hydroseeding will be used in areas that can be safely accessed with
hydroseeding equipment and in other areas determined appropriate by the EI or Transwestern’s
Representative.

Hydroseeding equipment will be equipped with sufficient tanks, pumps, nozzles, and other devices required
for mixing and hydraulically applying the seed, wood fiber mulch, and tackifier mix in slurry form onto the
prepared ground. The hydroseeding equipment will have built-in agitators which will keep the seed, mulch,
tackifier, and water mixed homogeneously until pumped from the tank. Hydroseeding and hydromulching
will occur in one application unless Transwestern’s Representative directs that they occur as two separate
applications.

Where hydroseeding and hydromulching occur as two applications, the hydroseeding slurry will contain
tackifier at 25 percent of the manufacturer’s recommended rate and 300 pounds of wood fiber mulch to
mark the seeded locations and the evenness of the application. The hydromulching will occur immediately
following hydroseeding on the same day, where feasible. Hydroseeding and hydromulching will be done
from two directions (e.g., left and right or up and down), where possible, to ensure maximum coverage of
the soil. Tackifiers will be used with the hydromulch at the manufacture’s recommended rates. Various
hydromulch products are available (see Section 11.12).

Hydroseeding will occur at the rates specified for broadcast seeding plus any adjustment the hydroseeding
company recommends based on equipment specifications.

11.12 Mulch

To enhance revegetation success, mulch (weed free straw, wood fiber hydromulch, native woody material)
will be applied on all disturbed areas. Mulch may also include surface rock if the regraded areas have similar
coverage (size, density and distribution) as adjacent undisturbed areas. Mulch reduces runoff and wind and
water erosion, moderates soil temperature, and reduces evaporation. Mulch also minimizes soil crusting
and improves infiltration of water and air and nutrients into the soil and enhances revegetation success
(Zeedyk and Jansens 2009).

Straw Mulch

Straw mulch will be CWF by the appropriate state certification program. Any straw that is found to contain
noxious weeds during application will be immediately removed from the construction right-of-way and
staging areas and properly disposed of in a public landfill. The EI or Transwestern’s Representative will
approve all straw.

The mulch will be uniformly applied at a rate of 2 tons/acre to cover the ground surface. Mulching will
occur immediately after seeding where broadcast or drill seeding occurs. The straw will be anchored by
crimping it into the soil with appropriate equipment. Liquid mulch binders are not expected to be utilized
unless hydromulch is applied.

Wood Fiber Mulch

Manufactured wood fiber mulch will be applied as hydromulch at a minimum of 2,000 pounds/acre during
hydroseeding, or at the rate recommended by product manufacturers based on site-specific conditions. A
tackifier or bonding agent recommended by the manufacturer will be used to bond the wood fiber mulch to
the soil surface.

The wood fiber mulch will consist of pure wood fibers manufactured expressly from virgin wood chips.
The chips will be processed in such a manner as to contain no trace of lead paint, varnish, printing ink,
petroleum-based compounds, or seed germination inhibitors. Fiber will not be produced from unknown
origin including recycled cellulose material such as sawdust, paper, cardboard, or residue from chlorine
bleached paper mills.

Wood fibers of mulch must maintain uniform suspension in water under agitation. The wood fiber mulch
will blend with seed and tackifier to form homogenous slurry. Upon application, the mulch will form a
blotter-like mat covering the ground. This mat will have the characteristics of water absorption and
percolation and will cover and bond grass seed in contact with the soil. The wood fiber mulch will be dyed
green to aid in visual metering during application. The dye will be non-toxic, biodegradable, and will not
inhibit plant growth.

Various hydromulch products are available for use depending on the site-specific conditions, such as areas
on steep and rugged topographic areas. Where determined appropriate by the EI or Transwestern’s
Representative, products such as Bonded Fiber Matrix, described below, or other similar products may be
used.

Bonded Fiber Matrix

Transwestern may use a bonded fiber matrix (BFM), or similar product, on slopes greater than 2.5 to 1 (i.e.,
40 percent), or where prescribed by the EI or Transwestern’s Representative. BFM is similar to wood fiber
mulch, but it has properties that allow it to remain strong and insoluble after its initial drying. BFM reduces


DESERT SOUTHWEST EXPANSION PROJECT                     22                  TRANSWESTERN PIPELINE COMPANY, LLC
                                                     DRAFT                                                ECRP



erosion by a) absorbing the impact of rainfall while still allowing water to filter through, and b) absorbing
water like a sponge to prevent overland water flow and rilling (Mat, Inc. 2017). It creates a strong and
durable mat of interlocking fiber strands held together by a bonding agent which is water resistant and
which will withstand re-exposure to moisture without re-dissolving or losing its adhesive quality. Once
dry, it forms a water-absorbent protective mat which is porous and breathable and secures soil and seed
until vegetation is established (Mat, Inc. 2017).

BFM is designed to mix and flow easily when wet and yet remain strong and insoluble once dry, protecting
the soil surface from repeated rains and sheet flows. BFM can be applied prior to a rainy season or late in
the year as it is formulated to endure the harsh conditions (Hydroseeding.info. 2026). In time, BFM
biodegrades completely into natural organic compounds which are beneficial to plant life. It is safe to use
in riparian zones and watersheds. Because BFM is sprayed on, the site remains relatively undisturbed,
further reducing the risk of erosion (Hydroseeding.info. 2026).

Within the Hot Springs-Swamp Springs Area of Critical Environmental Concern (ACEC) (MPs 435.5 to
437.7), Transwestern will utilize BFM or similar products where straw mulch is not applied.

Native Mulch

The native vegetative material cleared from the construction right-of-way and incorporated into the surface
soil may provide equivalent and effective mulch cover once respread over the disturbed areas depending
on the quantity/coverage of the material. Mulch may include woody, herbaceous, and rocky materials and
will be considered equivalent where it provides a surface coverage of approximately 75 percent of the
ground surface, as determined by the EI or Transwestern’s Representative according to site-specific
conditions.

11.13 Erosion Control Fabric

Transwestern will install erosion control fabric (such as jute or Excelsior) on streambanks at the time of
recontouring (see Figures 17, 18, and 19 in Attachment C) as directed by the EI or Transwestern’s
Representative. Erosion control fabric netting will be loose-weave 100 percent biodegradable natural
fibers. The fabric will be anchored using staples or other appropriate devices. The erosion control fabric
to be used on streambanks and steep slopes will be designed for the proposed use and will be approved by
the EI. The EI or Transwestern’s Representative will also determine other appropriate areas along the
construction rights-of-way where erosion control fabric will be applied based on site-specific conditions,
such as steep slopes or reestablished ditches or drainages.

12.0    STEEP AND RUGGED TERRAIN

The route was selected to be co-located to the extent practicable with other pipelines, and for the most part
avoids steep and rugged terrain. As described in Resource Report 6, more than 97 percent of the mainline
and 99 percent of the laterals are characterized by relatively gentle slopes of less than 33 percent (3H:1V).
Areas of steep to very steep terrain (greater than 50 percent; 2H:1V) are relatively short and highly localized
segments, representing less than one percent of the Project. The segments correspond to isolated
topographic features such as canyon walls, stream crossings, or short, steep upland slopes. Resource Report
6 also assessed where the Project crosses steep and very steep side slopes and require special consideration
during design and construction because the construction corridor in these areas requires significant cuts and
fills. This assessment identified six areas totaling 0.9 mile. As outlined in Resource Report 6, to reduce
the risk of construction-related adverse impacts to slope stability, the following mitigation measures will
be implemented during Project design and construction.

13.0    NOXIOUS WEED CONTROL PLAN

Transwestern has developed a Noxious Weed and Invasive Plant Management Plan to minimize the
establishment and spread of noxious weeds and invasive plants during and after Project construction (see
Attachment E). The plan describes the noxious weeds identified during Project surveys, and the potential
pre-construction management treatments that may be conducted prior to construction to minimize potential
spread. The plan includes equipment inspection and cleaning requirements and Project training and
compliance responsibilities. BMPs are outlined in the plan to minimize the potential spread of noxious
weeds from clearing and grading in areas of noxious weeds, the use of weed free materials, and the
restoration measures prescribed in this ECRP to promptly replant disturbed areas with appropriate seed
mixtures that will help prevent noxious weed establishment. Post-construction monitoring and reporting
are described as well as post-construction weed management measures that will be implemented.

14.0    MAINTENANCE

As outlined in Transwestern’s FERC Plan (see Section VII.A) Transwestern will conduct follow-up
inspections of all disturbed areas after the first and second growing seasons to determine the success of
revegetation. Transwestern will monitor crops for at least two years to determine the need for additional
restoration, unless the easement agreement specifies otherwise. Revegetation will be considered successful
in upland areas, if upon visual survey the density and cover of non-nuisance vegetation are similar in density
and cover to adjacent undisturbed lands. If vegetative cover and density are not similar or there are
excessive weeds after two full growing seasons, Transwestern will continue revegetation efforts until
revegetation is successful. Repair of erosion control structures will occur until the right-of-way has
successfully revegetated and has stabilized. Once the site is stabilized, temporary erosion control measures
will be removed. Transwestern will monitor and correct problems with drainage and irrigation systems
resulting from construction in agricultural areas until restoration is deemed successful.

Transwestern will test, operate, and maintain the proposed facilities in accordance with 49 CFR Part 192
and other applicable federal and state regulations. The mainline and lateral rights-of-way will be clearly
marked where they cross public roads, railroads, rivers, fenced property lines, and other locations as
necessary. All pipeline facilities will be marked and identified in accordance with applicable regulations
to avoid accidental excavation. During the operational life of the mainline and laterals, Transwestern’s
personnel will be responsible for any unforeseen erosion or potential mass movement that may occur.

I.       APPLICABILITY

         A.      The intent of this Plan is to identify baseline mitigation measures to minimize
                 erosion and enhance revegetation. Transwestern has identified measures
                 considered unnecessary, technically infeasible, or unsuitable based on the
                 Project location in west Texas, southwest New Mexico, and eastern Arizona and
                 has described alternatives applicable to the desert environment crossed by the
                 Project.

                 If necessary, Transwestern, upon authorization of the Project, will request
                 approval from the Director of the Office of Energy Projects (Director) for any
                 further changes through FERC’s variance process. Prior to requesting a
                 variance, Transwestern will ensure that the variance request:

                 1.      provides equal or better environmental protection;

                 2.      is necessary because a portion of this Plan is infeasible or unworkable
                         based on project-specific conditions; or

                 3.      is specifically required in writing by another federal, state, or Native
                         American land management agency for the portion of the project on its
                         land or under its jurisdiction.

                 Project-related impacts on wetland and waterbody systems are addressed in
                 Transwestern’s Wetland and Waterbody Construction and Mitigation Procedures
                 (Procedures).

                 As noted in Transwestern’s Procedures, only two wetlands will be crossed; they
                 are associated with the Pecos River and Salt Creek crossings in Texas. Survey
                 delineations in New Mexico and Arizona noted no wetlands. Two perennial
                 waterbodies were delineated in Texas (Pecos River at MP 31.33 and Salt Creek
                 at MP 43.74), and no perennial waterbodies were delineated in New Mexico and
                 Arizona. The Pecos River and Salt Creek and their associated wetlands in Texas
                 will be crossed by HDD as well as the Central Arizona Project (CAP) and Pima
                 Canals (man-made features with artificial perennial flow) in Arizona. Surveys
                 delineated ephemeral or intermittent open water features; they include 24 man-
                 made stock ponds and 13 playas, which are expected to be dry at the time of
                 construction. Because the dry washes, stock ponds, and playas are expected to be
                 dry at the time of construction, they will be crossed using typical cross-country
                 construction methods.

         F.      TEMPORARY EROSION CONTROL

                 Dry wash crossings will be completed using typical upland construction methods.
                 Average rainfall across the Project ranges between 7 and 13 inches. Over half of
                 the annual rainfall occurs during the monsoon season between mid-June through
                 September with the wettest period typically occurring between mid-July through
                 August 1. Rain events typically occur as short-duration high intensity thunder
                 showers that may result in runoff and flash flooding.

                 To minimize the potential for construction across dry washes occurring during
                 runoff/flash flooding events, Transwestern’s EIs, Company Representative, and
                 construction contractor would monitor upcoming weather forecasts to determine
                 if significant rainfall is anticipated at times when construction across dry washes
                 is planned. To the extent practicable, Transwestern would avoid installing the
                 pipeline across dry washes during periods of anticipated rainfall. If rainfall is
                 not expected to be significant (e.g., less than 0.5 inch) and Transwestern
                 determines that construction should proceed, environmental crews would be
                 notified of the location of planned crossings and would be available to respond
                 quickly if additional erosion control devices are required. If flow conditions
                 develop during construction of a given dry wash crossing, Transwestern’s EIs
                 and environmental crews would be notified immediately to determine the extent
                 of the flow and would install additional erosion control devices as necessary. If
                 flows are significant, and siltation is likely to occur, work would be stopped until

I.           APPLICABILITY

        A.      The intent of these Procedures is to minimize the extent and duration of Project-
                related disturbance to wetlands and waterbodies. Transwestern has identified
                measures considered unnecessary, technically infeasible, or unsuitable because
                of the Project’s location in west Texas, southwest New Mexico, and eastern
                Arizona, and has described alternatives in these Procedures that are applicable
                to that desert environment. Project-related impacts on non-wetland areas are
                addressed in Transwestern’s Upland Erosion Control, Revegetation, and
                Maintenance Plan (Plan).

                Only two wetlands will be crossed, and they are associated with the only two
                perennial waterbodies delineated for the Project (both in Texas: Pecos River/MP
                31.33 and Salt Creek/MP 43.74). No other wetlands were delineated. To avoid
                impacts, the Pecos River and Salt Creek and their associated wetlands will be
                crossed by HDD.

                Except for the Pecos River and Salt Creek in Texas and except for the Central
                Arizona Project (CAP) and several canals (man-made features with artificial
                perennial flow) in Arizona, all other waterbodies crossed by the Project are
                classified as intermittent or ephemeral dry washes. Trenchless crossing methods
                (HDD, direct pipe, or conventional bore) will be used to cross the CAP and several
                canals in Arizona, as well as the Rio Grande and San Pedro rivers, which are
                intermittent waterbodies. Other irrigation canals and ditches not crossed by
                trenchless crossing methods will be crossed according to the irrigation district or
                landowner specifications.

                The ephemeral or intermittent open water features crossed by the Project, include
                24 man-made stock ponds and 13 playas, which are all expected to be dry at the
                time of construction. Because the dry washes, stock ponds, and playas are expected
                to be dry at the time of construction, they will be crossed using typical cross-
                country construction methods.

                If necessary, Transwestern, upon authorization of the Project, will request approval
                from the Director of the Office of Energy Projects (Director) for any further
                changes to these Procedures through FERC’s variance process. Prior to requesting
                a variance, Transwestern will ensure that the variance request:

                  1.      provides equal or better environmental protection;

                  2.      is necessary because a portion of these Procedures is infeasible or
                          unworkable based on project-specific conditions; or

                                 feet wide but less than or equal to 100 feet wide at the water’s
                                 edge at the time of crossing; and

                         c.      “major waterbody” includes all waterbodies greater than 100 feet

  The following seed mixtures have been prepared based on the Project biological surveys, NRCS
  SSURGO data and ecological site data, seed vendor information, various seed mixture development tools
  and native plant databases (i.e., Bamert Seed Company 2026, EcoRestore Portal 2026, Caesar Kleberg
  Wildlife Research Institute 2026, The Arizona Native Plant Society 2026, and Native Plant Society of
  Texas 2026), and agency recommendations. The species selected are native species adapted to the project
  area that are commercially available; however, supplies may be limited and vary by year. The seed
  mixtures were developed with the primary intent to stabilize disturbed areas, control erosion, and inhibit
  establishment of invasive species. They are based on precipitation ranges, soil characteristics, and
  vegetation types so that disturbed areas are returned to preconstruction land uses as quickly as possible.
  Depending on the availability of commercially available seed species at the time of restoration, it may be
  necessary to use alternative seeding species or adjust the seeding rates of the available species in the
  mixtures. The seeding rates are based on 40 seeds per square foot using the NRCS’ Critical Area
  Conservation Practice Implementation Requirements 342 excel worksheet provided by New Mexico
  NRCS. The seed mixtures are subject to adjustments or consolidation based on further consultation and
  research. Seed mixtures are noted by mainline mileposts (MPs), and laterals are noted within seed

(2) Initial filing requirements. The initial application must include the documentation of initial cultural

     SHPOs, THPOs and land-managing agencies, if available. The initial cultural resources consultations

          inaccessible lands may be filed after a certificate is issued.
