                              4.0      CULTURAL RESOURCES

4.1     INTRODUCTION
Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
Commission) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act to construct, own, and operate the proposed
Desert Southwest Expansion Project (Project). The Project is an expansion of the existing Transwestern
system that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline (mainline) and
approximately 180.0 miles associated with 13 lateral pipelines (laterals), as well as new compressor stations
(CS), associated meter and regulator stations (M&R), and other aboveground facilities located in Texas,
New Mexico, and Arizona.
Resource Report 4 provides information regarding cultural resources including properties that are eligible
for or may be eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) that could be affected
by the construction and operation of the proposed Project. It summarizes the efforts that Transwestern has
taken to assist FERC and other agencies in meeting their obligations under the National Historic
Preservation Act (NHPA). It also discusses the results of background studies, Class III cultural resources
survey investigations, agency consultation and Native American outreach, and the plan for addressing
potential unanticipated discoveries and/or the discovery of human remains during Project-related activities.

4.2     COMMUNICATION WITH AGENCIES AND FEDERALLY RECOGNIZED
        TRIBES
4.2.1   State and Local Agency Communication and Consultation
Communications with applicable state and local agencies has occurred at various stages since the Project
began. Communications include Project introduction meetings, permit approvals, pre-field work plan
approvals, and survey permissions. These communications are outlined in Table 4.2-1.
In support of FERC’s National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and NHPA obligations, Transwestern
provided the participating state and local agencies with a copy of the applicable survey reports on September
14, 17, and 22, 2026, and requested concurrence with the proposed NRHP eligibility and management
recommendations. Review of the reports are ongoing, and concurrence and comments will be submitted to
FERC upon receipt. Copies of the transmittals and survey reports are provided in Appendix 4C.

4.3.1   Area of Potential Effects
4.3.1.1 Direct Effects APE
Consistent with FERC regulations and Section 106 of the NHPA, Transwestern is required to make a
reasonable and good faith effort to identify historic properties within the Project’s Area of Potential Effect
(APE) and to take into account any potential effects, direct or indirect, that the proposed undertaking could
have on properties listed or considered eligible for listing in the NRHP.
The APE is defined as the “geographic area or areas within which an undertaking may directly or indirectly
cause alterations in the character or use of historic properties, if any such properties exist” (36 Code of
Federal Regulations [CFR] § 800.16[d]). The APE is determined by the lead federal agency and considers
all areas of construction, such as pipeline right-of-way, aboveground facility sites, staging areas, extra
workspace areas, contractor yards, access roads, and other ancillary facilities. In support of the agency APE
determination, a 400-foot environmental survey area (ESA) along the proposed Project centerline for
mainline and 300-foot or 400-foot ESA for laterals (depending on pipe dimensions) was inventoried
regardless of previous survey. A 100-foot buffer around all proposed block infrastructure was inventoried
to allow adequate buffers and to comply with agency guidelines. Once improvement locations along
proposed access roads are identified, an ESA width will be determined based on the nature and extent of
the proposed disturbance. For the purposes of this report, the APE includes all areas of workspace across
the Project identified to date. However, the Project footprint is still being finalized, surveys are ongoing,
and avoidance options are being considered. If additional workspace is identified that may otherwise
impact sites currently avoided, the management recommendations will be revised to account for and address
all anticipated Project effects. A detailed description of the Project is provided in Resource Report 1.
4.3.1.2 Indirect Effects APE
The APE for indirect effects is considered to be the geographic areas from which any permanent
infrastructure has the potential to impact, diminish or alter the visual, auditory, vibratory, or atmospheric
setting of an NRHP listed or NRHP-eligible property (36 CFR § 800.16(d), 36 CFR § 800.5(a)(2)(v)). An
assessment of indirect effects for all aboveground facilities is ongoing, and the results will be included in a
supplemental filing.

4.3.2   Background Research
The following section provides a state-by-state summary of the background research conducted for the
Project. The survey reports in Appendix 4C provide more detailed discussions of the research.
4.3.2.1 Texas
A search of the Texas Archaeological Sites Atlas (TASA [2026]) database was conducted, prior to field
survey, to identify previous projects and archaeological sites within 1 kilometer (km) of the Project. A
review of historic maps and aerial photographs was also performed to find historic structures and/or
associated archaeological sites within the research area.
A total of 79 previous projects and 149 sites have been recorded within the research area. In general, the
densest concentration of sites come from the Fort Bliss and El Paso area near the Texas/New Mexico
Stateline. Prehistoric sites far outnumber historic sites and include dozens of artifact scatters (primarily
lithics), sites with hearth features, and lithic quarry/procurement sites. Examples of resources found at
historic sites include artifact scatters, an abandoned railroad, structural remnants, the old Carlsbad-El Paso
Highway, and an abandoned buried communication cable from the 1940s. A few State Antiquities
Landmark (SAL) sites are within 1 km of the research area: Firecracker Pueblo (41EP25), Hueco Tanks
State Park (41EP2), and several sites in western Culberson County. Many of the sites identified within the
Class I were originally recorded during the All-American Pipeline (AAPL) project in 1985 and the Pacific-
Texas Pipeline (Pac-Tex) project in 1987, though several of these lack polygonal boundaries.
4.3.2.2 New Mexico
Prior to field efforts, a Class I literature review was completed to identify previous investigations and
cultural resources recorded within a 0.3-mile (mi) (0.5 km) radius of the ESA. Data were derived from the
New Mexico Historic Preservation Division (NMHPD) New Mexico Cultural Resources Information
System (NMCRIS) and the NRHP geographic information system (National Park Service [NPS] 2026).
Additionally, U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) topographic maps, other historical maps, and aerial imagery,
were analyzed to identify potential historic features or other points of interest prior to field survey. These
sources provided information on previous archaeological investigations, recorded archaeological sites,
Historic Cultural Properties Inventories (HCPIs), and State Resources (SRs) listed in or eligible for listing
in the NRHP. The data was synthesized to determine the likelihood of encountering intact archaeological
deposits across the ESA. In total, 303 archaeological survey projects have been conducted within the study
area, and 307 archaeological sites have been previously recorded. Site types include prehistoric habitation
areas, campsites, artifact scatters, and historic roads, utility lines, irrigation ditches, and railroads.
4.3.2.3 Arizona
Prior to survey in Arizona, a Class I literature review was conducted of the digital records on file in
AZSITE, maps and records on file at the Arizona State Museum (ASM) Archaeological Records Office
(ARO), BLM Tucson, Safford, and Lower Sonoran Field Offices, Arizona Department of Transportation
(ADOT) portal, survey plats and patents on file with the BLM General Land Office (GLO), historical maps
from the USGS, aerial imagery, land-status information, Arizona Department of Water Resources well data,
and available mineral-resource data. In anticipation of realignments in the ESA, all site and project records
within 0.5 mile of the ESA were examined.
Review of relevant records indicated that 277 projects have been conducted within the research area. As a
result of these, 541 sites have been documented. Many of the sites were recorded in anticipation of
construction of the AAPL (today managed by El Paso Natural Gas [EPNG]). Documentation of these sites
is often inadequate, and in many cases, different agencies (for example, ASM as opposed to BLM) have
georeferenced site boundaries from AAPL field site records at different locations. Sites include prehistoric
habitation areas, mounds, and pithouses, and historic homesteads, utility lines, canals, and roads.

4.3.3   Methods
The following section provides a summary of state-by-state survey methods utilized for the Project. The
survey reports in Appendix 4C provide additional information.
4.3.3.1 Texas
Survey was conducted in accordance with the Council of Texas Archeologists (CTA) (2020) standards for
survey, which have been accepted by the Texas Historical Commission. At the start of fieldwork by Gray
& Pape, a pedestrian survey was completed across nine transects spaced 15 meters (m) apart and shovel
tests were excavated along three of the transects at 200 m intervals. After nearly 800 shovel tests had been
excavated, adjustments were made to this methodology. Through coordination with the Texas Historical
Commission (THC), the transects were reduced to seven total spaced 15 m apart, and shovel testing was
reduced to only along the mainline at 200 m intervals and in high probability areas at the point of intersect
(PI) or Field Lead’s discretion. The Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) Hybrid Potential
Archaeological Liability Map (HPALM) for the El Paso District was referred to when determining
archaeologically high potential areas. The HPALM is the result of a geographic information system (GIS)-
based, geoarchaeological predictive model of the apparent prehistoric site potential throughout the region
(Abbott 2021). Generally, high potential areas were defined as areas relatively close (<300 m) to water
sources, specifically on shoulder slopes, on alluvial and colluvial fans, near upland edges adjacent to
alluvial valleys, and near stream confluences. The survey transects are oriented with the path of the ESA.
Shovel tests were 30 centimeter (cm) in diameter and dug in 20-cm levels or less. Sediments were screened
through ¼ inch (in) hardware cloth unless high clay or water content prevented screening; in which the
sediments were troweled through by hand. The crew excavated shovel tests to subsoil, or to a minimum
depth of 80 cm, which ever came first. A handheld global positioning system (GPS) receiver was used to
mark the locations of shovel tests and other elements. The composition, texture, and color of the sediments
were recorded. The Munsell Soil Color Chart was used to identify soil colors (Munsell Color Company
2010). As part of the pedestrian survey, the field crew recorded observations on vegetation, ground
exposures, disturbances, soil types, geology, structures, and any artifacts or features encountered in the
survey area.
An archaeological site was defined as cultural material greater than 50 years of age characterized by the
following:
    •   ten or more artifacts of any class or type within a 15-m area, except for fire-cracked rock or when
        all pieces appear to originate from a single source (i.e., one ceramic pot drop, one broken glass
        bottle). However, single knapping episodes were treated as a site.
    •   one or more datable archaeological features with or without associated artifacts; or
    •   two or more undatable archaeological features (within 30 m of each other); or
    •   a single undatable feature with any associated artifacts
In general, 30 m is the maximum distance between manifestations, beyond which the materials are treated
as spatially unrelated. Identified cultural materials that did not meet these criteria were recorded as Isolated
Occurrences (IOs). While not classified as sites, the type and quantity of materials, the size and shape of
the feature, any construction details, probable function, and any relationship to nearby cultural materials
were recorded. These are described in the survey report tabularly (see Appendix 4C) with a paragraph
summary and representative photographs.
Site boundaries were determined within the ESA, with the extent of surface scatters being used to delineate
sites. Shovel testing was also conducted at sites with potential for subsurface deposits. Positive shovel tests
were delineated in a cruciform pattern at no more than 15 m intervals until two negative shovel tests were
excavated in each direction or Project/topographic limits were reached. Sites were also photographed from
a minimum of two angles. The location of artifacts, shovel tests, features, and site boundaries were captured

4.3.3.2 New Mexico
Terracon conducted a Class III pedestrian survey between February 12 and April 21, 2026. The survey was
performed in accordance with the guidelines outlined in the New Mexico Administrative Code (NMAC)
Title 4, Chapter 10, Part 15.11 and Part 15.12; the Procedures for Performing Cultural Resource Fieldwork
on Public Lands in the Area of New Mexico BLM Responsibilities (BLM Manual Supplement H-8100-1,
New Mexico, Oklahoma and Texas 2005); and protocols established during interagency consultations prior
to the fieldwork.
Terracon completed a 100 percent pedestrian survey of the ESA, walking transects spaced, on average, 15
m (49 feet [ft]) apart. Intervals were reduced at the discretion of supervisory personnel when the terrain,
vegetative cover, or nature of cultural properties (if present) necessitated smaller transect widths. Survey
of lands owned by the New Mexico State Land Office (NMSLO) or private entities was performed under
the general supervision of individuals listed in the SHPO directory of qualified supervisory personnel
(4.10.8.11 NMAC). Survey of BLM-managed segments of the ESA was performed under the direct
supervision of a qualified BLM cultural resource specialist or BLM-permitted Field Supervisor.
Archaeological sites were defined as cultural resources at least 50 years old (including a fixed feature) or a
concentration of 10 or more artifacts within a 20-m (65.6-ft) radius. If encountered, cultural resources that
did not meet these criteria (i.e., single artifacts, isolated features, sparse concentrations of less than 10
artifacts, or a concentration of artifacts from the same vessel) were recorded as IOs.
Archaeological sites were recorded to the extent permissible based on landownership (i.e., constrained to
the ESA on privately-owned land). If a site extended beyond the ESA on privately-owned land, Terracon
documented observations about features outside of, but visible from, the ESA. If large sites extended
outside the ESA, Terracon recorded all features and artifacts within and immediately adjacent to the ESA
and made observations about features outside of, but visible from, the ESA. Sites that extended beyond the
ESA on state- or BLM-managed lands were recorded until a 15-meter (m) gap without artifacts could be
established.
The investigation had a “no-collection” policy; therefore, artifacts (if encountered) were documented in the
field, but not collected. In-field analysis on all or a sample of all classes of surface-visible artifacts
including—but not limited—to lithics, ceramics, and historic artifacts was completed. The size of the
sample was sufficient to document the full variety of types of artifacts represented at the site and to delineate
intra-site activity areas as needed. Cultural materials encountered were described, photographed with a
scale, and then returned to their approximate origin. If necessary, additional documentation included
photographs of sites and features with appropriate scales, artifact and feature sketches, digital mapping,
field notes (e.g., surface visibility, site condition and size, depositional environment, source(s) of
disturbance, as applicable), and the completion of Laboratory of Anthropology (LA) site forms. A Global
Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) capable of sub-meter accuracy was used to record site locations,
features, point-located artifacts, and other Project elements.
Shovel tests (based on professional judgment) were placed in high probability areas to determine the
subsurface potential of sites with indeterminate NRHP eligibility based on pedestrian survey data. Shovel
tests excavated on BLM-managed lands measured 30 centimeters (cm) (12 inches [in]) in diameter, while

4.3.3.3 Arizona
In Arizona, Desert Archaeology and MCA conducted fieldwork between January 26 and July 8, 2026. The
surveys were conducted following ASM, BLM, and U.S. Forest Service (USFS) survey guidelines and site
recording standards. The project area was systematically transected by archaeologists walking in parallel
20-m-wide transects (ASLD, BLM, private) or 15-m-wide transects (USFS or higher site density areas).
The purpose of the pedestrian survey was to identify historic or precontact artifacts or features within the
project area. All finds were documented as either an archaeological site or as an IO if they did not meet site
criteria due to insufficient artifact quantity and/or diversity and the absence of associated features. The
ASM defines a site as containing the physical remains of past human activity at least 50 years old and
consisting of at least one of the following: (1) 20 or more artifacts from at least two material classes in a
15-m-diameter area; (2) 30 or more artifacts from a single material class in a 15-m-diameter area; (3) one
or more features in association with any number of artifacts; or (4) two or more associated features without
artifacts (ASM 1993, Bacon et. al 1995).
Per ASM’s revised site definition policies (Arizona Historical Archaeology Advisory Committee 2019,
ASM 2016), maintained historical constructions (e.g., roads, transmission lines, buildings) were
documented as in-use historic structures in accordance with Arizona SHPO (2019) guidelines. Previously
documented structures with an ASM site designation were recorded on the historic in-use structure form
(HISF) if they were determined to no longer meet the revised ASM site definition. Historic in-use structures
exempt from further documentation (e.g., historic natural gas pipelines, historic rail properties) were
excluded. Isolated features, such as unimproved roads that are unnamed in any records, were documented
as IOs. Single-episode historical waste dump features were not assigned site designations.
Survey performed on BLM-managed lands was conducted in accordance with guidelines set forth in BLM
Manual 8110 (BLM 2004) and the Programmatic Agreement between the Arizona SHPO and BLM-
Arizona (BLM 2014), in which BLM survey and reporting standards match those defined by the SHPO and

4.3.4   National Register Criteria
The National Register lists seven aspects that are evaluated to determine if a resource retains its integrity
(ability to convey completeness). The aspects of integrity required for NRHP eligibility are different for
each of the four NRHP Criteria. If a resource is being assessed for significance because of its association
with an event, then integrity of setting, feeling, and association is more important. If being assessed for
significance as an example of design, then integrity of location, design, materials, and workmanship are
more important. For more information, refer to How to Apply the National Register of Criteria for
Evaluation (NPS 1997). The seven aspects are as follows:
    •   Location: The actual place where a property was constructed or an event occurred.
    •   Design: The combination of elements that create a property's form, plan, space, structure, and style,
        including its organization of space, proportion, scale, and ornamentation.

    •   Setting: The physical environment of a historic property, which is crucial for understanding its
        historical role and character.
    •   Materials: The physical elements used to form the property during a specific period and in a specific
        pattern.
    •   Workmanship: The physical evidence of the crafts of a particular culture or people from a specific
        historical period.
    •   Feeling: The property's expression of the aesthetic or historic sense of a particular period.
    •   Association: The direct link between a historic property and a significant historical event or person.
The quality of significance is present in resources that “possess integrity of location, design, setting,
materials, workmanship, feeling, and association” and at least one of the following criteria:
        A: that are associated with events that have made a significant contribution to the broad patterns of
        our history; or
        B: that are associated with the lives of persons significant in our past; or
        C: that embody the distinctive characteristics of a type, period, or method of construction, or that
        represent the work of a master, or that possess high artistic values, or that represent a significant
        and distinguishable entity whose components may lack individual distinction; or
        D: that have yielded, or may be likely to yield, information important in prehistory or history (NPS
        1997).

4.5.1.4 Historic Cultural Properties Inventories (HCPIs)
Elephant Butte Irrigation District. The Elephant Butte Irrigation District was developed as part of the
US Reclamation Service (now Bureau of Reclamation/USBR) Rio Grande Project in 1903. It proved
enormously beneficial to farming in the area by greatly increasing the acreage of irrigated farmland in New
Mexico. Irrigation farming in the Rio Grande Valley was an extremely important component of the region’s
subsistence economy. Irrigation ventures spread north from El Paso in the 1800s, though they were often
impacted by flooding and channel shifts, necessitating frequent reconstruction. Such intensive efforts
limited viable farmland (Phillips 1997). The Elephant Butte Irrigation District diverted water throughout
the Mesilla and Rincon valleys, providing relief to farmers with waterlogged and flooded crops. The
irrigation system rebuilt many existing irrigation systems and helped regulate the unpredictable water table
and Rio Grande. The greater part of the Elephant Butte Irrigation District was constructed by 1921. In 1997,
Elephant Butte Irrigation District was listed in the NRHP under Criteria A and C. Nine segments of
irrigation ditches associated with the Elephant Butte District were documented within the proposed right-
of-way and avoidance is recommended. Construction crossing methods for these linear resources is still
being determined. If avoidance by trenchless crossing method is not possible, a treatment plan will be
prepared.
Unnamed Ditches. One unnamed ditch (HCPI 53557) was documented in the Project right-of-way and is
recommended not eligible.
Railroads. Segments of three railroads were also documented within the Project right-of-way: the
Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway/Burlington Northern and Santa Fe Railway; The Arizona and New
Mexico Railway; and the Southern Pacific Railroad.
Two segments of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe Railway/Burlington Northern and Santa Fe Railway
(HCPI 31896/47340) were previously determined eligible for the NRHP under Criteria A and C for its
importance as one of the first railway systems in the state that lead to the development of communities
throughout New Mexico. Both segments will be avoided by the HDD crossing of the Rio Grande River.
One segment of the Southern Pacific/Union Pacific railroad is located within the Project right-of-way
(HCPI 31362). The railroad has been previously determined eligible for the NRHP under Criterion A due

The remainder of the trails in the Desert Sun ESA group most closely with what Darling and Eiselt (2009)

they are poorly preserved. A portion of the Butterfield Overland Stage Route has been previously recorded
as AZ T:14:61(ASM)/AZ T:15:52(ASM). The portion intersecting the ESA is currently abandoned, but
satellite imagery clearly indicates that the track was improved for automobile traffic and used for many
years after the abandonment of the famous overland mail and stagecoach route used between 1857 and
1881.
Likewise, the digitized boundary of the Juan de Anza National Historic Trail intersects the current ESA,
but no trail alignment is visible in satellite imagery or during field surveys of what is now an irrigated
alfalfa field. The Juan De Anza trail, which was followed by the pioneering Spanish explorer Juan De Anza
in 1774 and 1776 to connect Sonora to Alta California, would have been a wide route of multiple parallel
tracks forged by Spanish military personnel accompanying their herds of cattle. Subsequent Spanish
expeditions following this track established seasonally shifting “high” and “low” roads along the Gila River
floodplain. Research goals related to the Juan de Anza trail corridor focus on identifying any Spanish-era
artifacts in the general vicinity of the route.

report's findings and recommendations.

                              6. GEOLOGICAL RESOURCES


6.1     INTRODUCTION

Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly-owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or
Commission) pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act to construct, own, and operate the proposed
Desert Southwest Expansion Project (Project). The Project is an expansion of the existing Transwestern
system that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline (mainline) and
approximately 180.0 miles associated with 13 lateral pipelines (laterals), as well as new compressor stations
(CS), associated meter and regulator (M&R) stations, and other aboveground facilities located in Texas,
New Mexico, and Arizona.

6.2     GEOLOGY

Appendix 6A provides the geological resources descriptions and effects analysis for the Project.

6.3     PALEONTOLOGICAL RESOURCES

A summary of the results of the Project paleontological resource analysis of existing data and field surveys
is provided in this section. Complete data are provided in the field survey reports for each state (see
Appendix 6B, filed as Privileged). The purpose of the field surveys was to identify scientifically important
and non-important paleontological resources within the project area based on geologic mapping, scientific
literature, museum records, and a pedestrian survey of potentially fossiliferous geographic areas and
geologic units. The field survey results were used to develop mitigation recommendations for the Project.
The detailed recommendations are provided in the Paleontological Resource Monitoring and Mitigation
Plan (see Appendix 6C).

The Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM’s) Potential Fossil Yield Classification (PFYC) System (BLM
2016) is a predictive resource management tool founded on two basic facts of paleontology: 1) occurrences
of paleontological resources are closely tied to the geologic units (i.e., formations, members, or beds) that
contain them; and 2) the likelihood of the presence of fossils can be broadly predicted from the distribution
of geologic units at or near the surface. Therefore, geologic mapping, as the documentation of geologic unit
distribution, is a reliable method for assessing the potential of geologic units to preserve fossils. PFYC
classifications are used to assess possible resource impacts and mitigation needs for federal actions that
involve surface disturbance, land use planning, or land tenure adjustment. Because of its demonstrated
value as a resource management tool, the PFYC has been utilized for many years for projects across the
country, regardless of agency or land ownership. The PFYC defines paleontological resource potential
based on a numeric ranking system from 1 (very low potential) to 5 (very high potential) and U (unknown
potential) (see Table 6.3-1).

Scientifically important paleontological localities are defined as those localities containing relatively
abundant, well preserved, and/or uncommon fossils. Fossils also potentially have economic value and those
on private property belong to the landowner.

Construction-related ground disturbance will take place during right-of-way grading, trenching,
construction of access roads and facilities, and during specialized construction techniques (i.e., horizontal
directional drilling). These activities have the potential to adversely impact scientifically and economically
important paleontological resources. With mitigation, these impacts can be reduced to below the level of
significance and may become beneficial impacts if mitigation results in the discovery, salvage, and
preservation of non-renewable paleontological resources and associated data.

In summary, one geologic unit has very low paleontological potential (PFYC 1), five have low
paleontological potential (PFYC 2), 12 have moderate paleontological potential (PFYC 3), three have high
paleontological potential (PFYC 4), and five have unknown paleontological potential (PFYC U).

Museum records combined with the field survey results demonstrate the potential for adverse impacts on
scientifically important subsurface paleontological resources during construction. According to museum
records, there are no previously recorded fossil localities confirmed within the project area. Other research
sources include the Paleobiology Database (PBDB), which lists a total of 833 fossil localities, and the
University of Texas El Paso, which has recorded 21 fossil localities within the six counties in Texas affected
by the Project. Additionally, the Texas Memorial Museum (TMM) (renamed the Texas Science & Natural
History Museum) and Jackson School of Geosciences Non-Vertebrate Paleontology Laboratory at the
University of Texas at Austin has recorded 6,344 invertebrate fossil specimens within the six counties.
Within 1 mile of the Project, 442 invertebrate fossil specimens were collected from the Bell Canyon, Cherry
Canyon, and Hueco formations. The TMM declined to provide data for vertebrate fossils.

During the pedestrian field survey, 13 scientifically important and 53 non-scientifically important fossil
localities were recorded. Of the scientifically important fossil localities, 11 are located on private lands, and
two are located on state lands owned by the University of Texas. Of the non-scientifically important fossil
localities, 40 are located on private lands, and 13 are located on state lands owned by the University of
Texas. No fossils were collected during the field survey.

In summary, four of the New Mexico geologic units have very low paleontological potential (PFYC 1),
seven have low paleontological potential (PFYC 2), three have high paleontological potential (PFYC 4),
one has very high paleontological potential (PFYC 5), and three have unknown paleontological potential
(PFYC U).

Museum records combined with the field survey results demonstrate the potential for adverse impacts on
scientifically important subsurface paleontological resources during construction. According to museum
records and additional data, there are three previously recorded fossil localities confirmed within the project
area and an additional three localities confirmed within 1-mile of the mainline. The New Mexico Museum
of Natural History and Science has 221 records of fossil specimens in Doña Ana County and 8 from Luna
County, including a mammoth tooth collected from within 1-mile of the Project. The University of Texas
El Paso has recorded 759 fossil specimens in Doña Ana County, three reported from unknown counties,
and no fossil localities have been reported within 1-mile of the Project. The PBDB lists 60 fossil localities
in Doña Ana County, 37 in Luna County, 41 in Grant County, and 173 in Hidalgo County. Because precise
geographic coordinates are not provided by the database, it is unknown whether any of these fossil localities
are located within the Project footprint.

During the pedestrian field survey, two scientifically important and 21 non-scientifically important fossil
localities were recorded. The two scientifically important fossil localities are located on BLM-managed
lands. The non-scientifically important fossil localities are located on BLM-managed and private lands. No
fossils were collected during the field survey.

In summary, six of the Arizona geologic units have high paleontological potential (PFYC 4), one has
unknown paleontological potential (PFYC U), four have low paleontological potential (PFYC 2), and five
have very low paleontological potential (PFYC 1).

Museum records combined with the field survey results demonstrate the potential for adverse impacts on
scientifically important subsurface paleontological resources during construction. According to museum
records, there are no previously recorded fossil localities within 1 mile of the Project. The Arizona Museum
of Natural History declined to perform a record search for the Project. The Arizona State Museum and the
New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science have no localities within the project area. The PBDB
has 165 previously recorded fossil localities within the counties affected by the Project: 123 in Cochise
County, 10 in Pima County, eight in Pinal County, three in Maricopa County, and 21 in Mohave County.
Because precise geographic coordinates are not provided by the PBDB, it is unknown whether any of the
fossil localities are located within the project area. The University of Texas El Paso has recorded 48
localities in Cochise County, 21 in Pima County, five in Pinal County, six in Maricopa County, and 21 in
Mohave County. None of these fossil localities are confirmed within the project area.

6.3.4   Impacts and Mitigation
Based on analyses of existing data and the results of Project field surveys, the following mitigation
recommendations will be implemented:

    1. Surveys will be completed in unsurveyed areas with paleontological potential;

    2. The plan for the Unanticipated Discovery of Paleontological Resources (see Appendix 6D) will
       be implemented; and

    3. The procedures described in the Paleontological Resource Monitoring and Mitigation Plan (see
       Appendix 6C) will be followed during construction. Monitoring recommendations are
       summarized as follows:

        Paleontological monitoring is typically required for PFYC 4, 5, and U geologic units on federal
        lands. Spot-checking is recommended for PFYC 3 geologic units. Monitoring is not recommended
        for PFYC 1 and 2 geologic units. Table 6.3-5 summarizes the mileages of PFYC classes per state
        calculated from the geologic and PFYC maps (see Appendix 6C).

1.0 Introduction
Transwestern Pipeline Company, LLC (Transwestern), a wholly owned subsidiary of Energy Transfer, LP
(Energy Transfer), is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
pursuant to Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act (NGA) to construct, own, and operate the proposed Desert
Southwest Expansion Project (Project). The Project is an expansion of the existing Transwestern system
that will consist of approximately 525.2 miles of 48-inch diameter mainline pipeline (mainline) and
approximately 180.0 miles associated with 13 lateral pipelines (laterals), as well as new compressor
stations, associated meter stations, and other aboveground facilities located in Texas, New Mexico, and
Arizona. The Project will provide firm transportation service of up to 2.3 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of
natural gas from the Permian Basin to delivery points serving customers in New Mexico and Arizona and
will upgrade Transwestern’s existing Phoenix Lateral to allow bi-directional flow.

This report was prepared to meet applicable FERC Resource Report 6 requirements by documenting
geologic conditions and hazards that could affect, or be affected by, the Project; evaluating associated risks
and impacts; and identifying appropriate avoidance, mitigation, monitoring, or additional investigation. The
evaluation also complies with Energy Transfer’s Geohazard Evaluations for New Projects standard through
Phase I and Phase II, including desktop analysis of available geologic data, light detection and ranging
(LiDAR) data, and aerial imagery to develop a geohazard inventory, followed by nonintrusive field
reconnaissance to characterize identified features and determine whether further evaluation or
management measures are warranted. The mainline and laterals are shown with respect to the surrounding
area in the attached Figure 1. Vicinity Map. This report describes the geologic hazards and mineral
resources associated with the Project.

3.0 Topographic Conditions
3.1        GENERAL TOPOGRAPHIC SETTING
The mainline begins at milepost (MP) 0 in western Texas and continues westerly for approximately 525
miles before terminating in south-central Arizona. The route crosses the Texas–New Mexico state line near
MP 200 and the New Mexico–Arizona state line near MP 362. Regionally, the mainline begins within the
Pecos Valley section of the Great Plains Physiographic Province and subsequently crosses the Sacramento,
Mexican Highland, and Sonoran Desert sections of the Basin and Range Physiographic Province.
Physiographic boundaries and transition mileposts are approximate because regional mapping is not
intended for project-scale delineation (Fenneman and Johnson 1946; USGS 2020).

Topography along the Project consists of broad desert basins, piedmont slopes, plateaus, isolated uplands,
and generally north- to northwest-trending mountain ranges. Long areas of flat to gently sloping basin
terrain are interrupted by shorter sections of moderate to steep relief near mountain fronts, bedrock ridges,
drainage corridors, and interbasin divides. Characteristic landforms include alluvial fans, coalesced fan
aprons or bajadas, bolsons, playas, pediments, terraces, and ephemeral washes. Consequently, elevation
changes generally occur as repeated ascents and descents between basin floors and adjacent uplands
rather than as a consistent east-to-west trend (National Park Service 2020).

Between MP 0 and approximately MP 45, the mainline traverses the Pecos Valley section of the Great
Plains Physiographic Province in western Texas. Terrain is predominantly level to gently undulating and
consists of broad alluvial and eolian surfaces with shallow swales, low ridges, localized dune fields, and
intermittent drainageways. The route crosses the Pecos River corridor near the eastern end of this segment.
Outside the river floodplain, drainage is sparse and primarily occurs through ephemeral channels that
convey runoff following precipitation events. Playas and internally drained depressions may occur on the
broader basin floor. Terrain becomes increasingly varied toward the west as the mainline approaches the
bedrock uplands of Trans-Pecos Texas (Texas Bureau of Economic Geology 1996a).

From approximately MP 45 to MP 214, the mainline crosses the Sacramento section of the Basin and
Range Physiographic Province through Trans-Pecos Texas and into southern New Mexico. This segment
contains greater topographic variation along the route and includes bedrock ranges, dissected uplands,
plateaus, broad intermontane basins, and extensive piedmont surfaces. Slopes are generally gentle on
distal alluvial fans and basin floors but become moderate to steep near mountain fronts, canyon mouths,
escarpments, and bedrock ridges. Rock outcrops, thin soils, colluvial slopes, and coarse fan deposits are
common in higher-relief areas. Drainage is dominated by arroyos and intermittent channels that descend
from the mountains and spread across alluvial fans. Many channels terminate within internally drained
basins or playas. The segment ends near the Rio Grande valley, which forms a broad regional topographic
low bordered by floodplain deposits, terraces, and piedmont slopes (Texas Bureau of Economic Geology
1996a; National Park Service 2020).

Between approximately MP 214 and MP 470, the route traverses the Mexican Highland section of the Basin
and Range Physiographic Province across southern New Mexico and southeastern Arizona. The landscape
consists of broad structural and alluvial basins separated by isolated mountain ranges and bedrock
uplands. Basin interiors support extended areas of nearly level to gently sloping terrain, while localized
moderate to steep relief occurs at mountain fronts, bedrock projections, and interbasin divides. Alluvial
fans and bajadas slope away from the ranges toward basin interiors and may be dissected by shallow to
moderately incised arroyos. Elevation changes are generally gradual across the basins but become more
pronounced along their margins.

Drainage throughout the Mexican Highland segment is primarily intermittent or ephemeral. Many washes
lose definition on distal fan surfaces or terminate in internally drained basins rather than connecting to
perennial rivers. Important drainage areas crossed by the Project include the Mimbres Basin in
southwestern New Mexico, the San Simon drainage near the New Mexico–Arizona state line, and the San
Pedro River Valley in southeastern Arizona. The San Pedro Valley forms a broad topographic low bordered
by alluvial terraces, fan deposits, and mountain piedmonts. Flash flooding, channel migration, sheet flow,
and sediment deposition may locally affect washes, fan surfaces, and basin low points (National Park
Service 2020).

From approximately MP 470 to the western terminus near MP 525, the mainline crosses the Sonoran
Desert section of the Basin and Range Physiographic Province in south-central Arizona. The terrain
generally becomes lower and more open toward the west, although isolated mountain fronts and bedrock
hills produce localized areas of moderate relief. Broad alluvial basins, gently inclined fan surfaces,
bajadas, floodplains, and ephemeral washes dominate the landscape. Surface materials are primarily
unconsolidated alluvium, with coarse deposits near mountain fronts grading to finer sediments within basin
interiors. The mainline crosses the Santa Cruz River corridor, a regional topographic low bordered by
terraces and broad piedmont slopes. Numerous tributary washes cross the route west of the river and
typically convey water only during or shortly after rainfall.

Overall, the Project transitions from the subdued terrain of the Pecos Valley through the rugged ranges and
broad bolsons of Trans-Pecos Texas and then across the alternating mountain ranges and desert basins of
southern New Mexico and Arizona. The most pronounced topographic conditions occur near mountain
fronts, bedrock uplands, interbasin divides, incised arroyos, and major river valleys. Although basin interiors
generally have gentle slopes, they may contain playas, flood-prone washes, unstable channels, dune fields,
and areas susceptible to sheet flow and sediment deposition.

4.0 Geologic Conditions
4.1          REGIONAL GEOLOGIC SETTING
The Project extends from the Delaware Basin of the greater Permian Basin in western Texas and
southeastern New Mexico, across the southern Rio Grande rift and Orogrande Basin of south-central New
Mexico, and through the Pedregosa Basin and Basin and Range Province of southeastern and south-central
Arizona. This regional framework records a long sequence of Precambrian crustal assembly, Paleozoic
marine deposition and basin development, Mesozoic contraction and magmatism, and Cenozoic extension
that produced the modern fault-bounded ranges and sediment-filled valleys.

The oldest rocks beneath and locally exposed along the Project are Proterozoic crystalline basement
composed principally of granitic plutons, metamorphic gneiss and schist, and volcanic and sedimentary
assemblages. These rocks formed during accretion of tectonostratigraphic terranes to southern Laurentia,
mainly between about 1.8 and 1.6 billion years ago, and were later modified by Mesoproterozoic
deformation and magmatism (Karlstrom and Bowring 1988). By late Precambrian to early Paleozoic time,
the region had become a comparatively stable continental margin.

During much of the Paleozoic Era, repeated marine transgressions covered the region with shallow seas.
Cambrian through Mississippian deposition produced widespread sandstone, shale, limestone, and
dolostone on broad shelves along the southern margin of Laurentia (Ross 1976). Pennsylvanian
deformation associated with the Ancestral Rocky Mountains fragmented the shelf into basement-cored



 File No. 18782-065-00
 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                             Page 7




uplifts and intervening basins, including precursors of the Delaware, Orogrande, and Pedregosa basins
(Kluth and Coney 1981). These basins accumulated thick carbonate and clastic successions, while
adjacent uplifts supplied locally coarse sediment.

Permian deposition was especially important in the Delaware Basin. A deep marine trough was bordered
by carbonate platforms and reef complexes, including the Capitan Reef exposed in the Guadalupe and
Apache Mountains (King 1948). Limestone, dolostone, sandstone, shale, and later evaporites accumulated
from deep-basin to shelf and restricted-lagoon environments. These strata form much of the bedrock
beneath the eastern portion of the Project and contain major petroleum reservoirs. Increasing aridity and
restricted circulation late in the Permian promoted widespread gypsum, anhydrite, and halite deposition;
dissolution of these evaporites locally influences modern karst and subsidence conditions.

During the Mesozoic Era, regional sedimentation shifted toward continental red beds, fluvial deposits, and
eolian sandstone, followed by development of an active continental margin along western North America.
Late Cretaceous through early Paleogene Sevier and Laramide deformation produced crustal shortening,
thrust and reverse faulting, basement-involved uplifts, and structural basins. In southern Arizona and New
Mexico, Laramide deformation was accompanied by widespread intrusive and volcanic activity related to
subduction along the continental margin (Dickinson 1981). Older Paleozoic and Mesozoic strata were
folded, faulted, uplifted, and locally removed by erosion.

The regional stress regime changed from contraction to extension during the Oligocene and Miocene.
Crustal stretching formed the Basin and Range Province and the southern Rio Grande rift, generating major
normal faults, uplifted mountain blocks, and downdropped grabens and half-grabens (Chapin and Cather
1994; Keller and Baldridge 1999). In southern New Mexico, rift-related subsidence formed basins such as
the Hueco Bolson and Mesilla Basin, which accumulated thick alluvial-fan, fluvial, lacustrine, and playa
deposits. In Arizona, locally large-magnitude extension produced detachment faults, metamorphic core
complexes, and widespread middle Tertiary volcanism (Spencer and Reynolds 1989). Basin fill across both
states generally consists of poorly consolidated gravel, sand, silt, and clay eroded from adjacent ranges
and may be thousands of feet thick.

Quaternary processes continue to modify the mainline and lateral segments through erosion, stream
incision, alluvial-fan deposition, eolian transport, and playa sedimentation. Modern surficial materials
include channel and floodplain alluvium along ephemeral drainages, piedmont deposits at mountain fronts,
playa clay and silt in internally drained basins, and localized dune sand. Although extension has slowed
since Miocene time, parts of the Rio Grande rift and Basin and Range Province remain tectonically active.
Overall, the present landscape reflects Precambrian basement overlain by Paleozoic marine strata,
deformed and intruded during Mesozoic to early Cenozoic contraction, and subsequently disrupted by
Cenozoic normal faulting and basin development.

4.2        BEDROCK GEOLOGY
Bedrock mapping by the Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona Geological Surveys (Texas Bureau of Economic
Geology 1996b; New Mexico Bureau of Geology and Mineral Resources 2003; Arizona Geological Survey
2026a) indicates the Project crosses geologic units ranging from Holocene surficial deposits to Proterozoic
crystalline basement rocks. In stratigraphic order from youngest to oldest, the route crosses the following
generalized units:

■ Holocene to late Pleistocene (~0 – 0.13 Ma) surficial deposits include modern alluvium, piedmont
      alluvial deposits, lacustrine/playa sediments, and young basin-fill deposits associated with active
      drainages and desert basins. These materials are typically unconsolidated sand, gravel, silt, and clay
      deposited in stream channels, floodplains, fans, and closed basins.
■ Pleistocene to Pliocene (~0.13 – 5.3 Ma) basin-fill and sedimentary units include older alluvial fan
      deposits, shallow basin fill, the Gila Group, Upper Santa Fe Group, and related upper Tertiary
      sedimentary rocks. These units consist mainly of conglomerate, sandstone, mudstone, and locally
      lacustrine deposits formed during Basin and Range extension and basin development.
■ Miocene to Oligocene (~5.3 – 34 Ma) volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks are widespread along the
      route and include basaltic to andesitic lava flows, rhyolitic lavas and tuffs, Datil Group ash-flow tuffs,
      volcaniclastic sedimentary aprons, and mixed volcanic-sedimentary successions. These rocks record
      extensive mid-Tertiary volcanism associated with regional crustal extension.
■ Upper Cretaceous to Paleogene (~34 – 100 Ma) volcanic rocks consist largely of andesitic to dacitic
      lava flows, pyroclastic breccias, and volcanic centers related to Laramide magmatism.
■ Jurassic to Cretaceous (~100 – 201 Ma) sedimentary rocks in Arizona include mixed sedimentary
      and minor volcanic units composed of conglomerate, sandstone, mudstone, and limestone deposited
      in continental and shallow marine environments.
■ Pennsylvanian and Permian (~252 – 323 Ma) sedimentary rocks exposed in west Texas include
      limestone-dominated units such as the Hueco Formation (or Group) and undivided Pennsylvanian
      strata representing marine shelf deposition along the ancestral Permian Basin margin.
■ Proterozoic (~1,100 – 1,800 Ma) crystalline basement rocks form the oldest units encountered and
      include Early Proterozoic metamorphic rocks and Middle Proterozoic granitic intrusions. These rocks
      represent ancient continental crust that was later uplifted during Basin and Range deformation.

4.3        EXCAVATION CHARACTERISTICS AND BLASTING
Blasting may be required for trench excavation in areas where hard, non-rippable bedrock occurs. The
bedrock units where blasting may be necessary are expected to consist primarily of igneous, volcanic and
metamorphic rocks which generally correspond to the areas with localized rugged terrain in western New
Mexico and Arizona. In addition, local areas of well-lithified sedimentary rock may need to be blasted.

For preliminary planning purposes, it is assumed that blasting will be required in areas where hard, non-
rippable bedrock occurs within 10 feet of the ground surface. These areas were identified by reviewing the
NRCS soils maps and descriptions to identify soil units that typically contain bedrock within 200 centimeters
(approximately 6.5 feet of the ground surface). Descriptions of soil shallow restrictive layers may be found
in Resource Report 7. This information and information from geologic maps and topographic relief were
subsequently used to estimate excavation characteristics along the Project by placing the mapped
subsurface conditions into one of the three following categories:

■ Class 1 – Mechanical – Soil: Defined by areas mapped as Quaternary alluvium where it is estimated
      that approximately 80 percent of the trench can be excavated by means of typical trenching equipment

    excavation using heavy class machinery (i.e., rock bucket, ripper, hydraulic hammer, trencher, or saw).
■ Class 2 – Mechanical (Rippable) – Bedrock: Defined by areas mapped as relatively soft bedrock such
    as sedimentary rock or welded tuff that may generally be mechanically excavated using heavy class
    machinery (i.e., rock bucket, ripper, hydraulic hammer, trencher, or saw). This category assumes
    10 percent typical soil trenching, 70 percent mechanical excavating/ripping, and 20 percent blasting

■ Class 3 – Blasting – Bedrock: Defined by areas mapped as relatively hard bedrock, including

7.1        SEISMIC HAZARDS
The primary seismic hazards to buried pipelines are related to permanent ground displacement from
ground surface fault rupture, differential settlement from soil liquefaction, lateral ground displacement
related to soil strength loss from liquefaction, and slope displacements triggered by ground shaking.
Earthquake ground shaking is only important as a triggering mechanism for liquefaction and slope
movement. Regional subsidence caused by groundwater or hydrocarbon withdrawal is not an earthquake-
induced hazard and is addressed in Section 7.5, Earth Fissures.

Surface fault rupture and liquefaction-induced hazards are ground displacement hazards, and they pose
the greatest risk to a buried pipeline because they impose localized differential ground movement on the
pipe. The severity of ground displacement hazards depends on several factors, including the magnitude of
the earthquake, the distance of the earthquake source from the pipeline (both lateral and vertical), soil and
rock conditions, and local topography. Potential surface fault rupture hazards can be considered to be
constrained to within 300 to 600 feet of mapped fault lineaments. Translating the ground shaking hazard
to a corresponding liquefaction, lateral spread, or slope displacement hazard requires subsurface
information from field investigations.

Seismic hazards were evaluated for the Project by reviewing available geologic maps showing mapped
faults, paleoseismic investigations of the fault zone, reviewing historic records of the size and location of
recorded earthquakes, and completing general analyses of the portions of the Project with potential for
surface fault rupture, liquefaction, and liquefaction-induced lateral spreading.

7.1.1            Seismotectonic Setting
The Project traverses several tectonic provinces with differing levels of seismic activity and seismic hazard.
The Project crosses portions of the stable Permian Basin, the tectonically active Rio Grande rift, and the
extensional Basin and Range Province of New Mexico and Arizona. Regional seismicity along the Project is
primarily associated with late Cenozoic normal faulting, crustal extension, localized magmatism, and, in
some areas, anthropogenic activity related to fluid injection and hydrocarbon production.

The eastern portion of the Project lies within the Delaware Basin of the greater Permian Basin region of
west Texas and southeastern New Mexico. Historically, this region was characterized by relatively low levels
of natural seismicity compared to more tectonically active regions farther west. However, seismic activity
in the Permian Basin has increased substantially during the past two decades, particularly in areas of
intensive oil and gas development and wastewater disposal (Frohlich et al. 2016). Many recent
earthquakes in west Texas and southeastern New Mexico are interpreted to be induced or triggered by
deep wastewater injection associated with hydrocarbon production. Although most induced earthquakes
are small to moderate magnitude events, several earthquakes greater than magnitude 5 have occurred in
the broader Permian Basin region in recent years (Ellsworth 2013). Seismicity in this portion of the Project
is therefore influenced by both inherited basement structures and ongoing anthropogenic stress
perturbations.

Westward across southern New Mexico, the Project enters the Rio Grande rift, one of the principal
tectonically active extensional provinces in the interior western United States. The Rio Grande rift is
characterized by north-trending normal faults, crustal thinning, elevated heat flow, and ongoing extensional
deformation (Keller and Baldridge 1999). Rift-related seismicity is associated primarily with Quaternary

 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                                 Page 15




normal fault systems that bound major structural basins, including portions of the Mesilla Basin and Hueco
Bolson. Earthquake activity within the Rio Grande rift is generally moderate but persistent, reflecting
continued crustal extension and reactivation of basin-bounding faults (Wong et al. 1995). Slip rates on
most faults in southern New Mexico are low relative to those on plate-boundary faults in California and
Nevada. Nonetheless, many of these faults show evidence of Quaternary displacement and are considered
potentially active.

The central and western portions of the Project traverse the Basin and Range Province of southern New
Mexico and Arizona, a broad region undergoing Cenozoic crustal extension characterized by fault-bounded
mountain ranges and sediment-filled basins. Seismicity within the Basin and Range Province is associated
primarily with normal faulting related to ongoing regional extension (Parsons 1995). Most earthquakes in
southeastern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico are low to moderate magnitude events distributed
across diffuse fault systems rather than concentrated along a single major plate-boundary structure.
Nevertheless, Quaternary faults capable of generating significant ground motion occur throughout the
region.

Several mapped Quaternary fault systems occur near, or cross, portions of the Project, particularly within
the Rio Grande rift and Basin and Range structural provinces. These faults are regionally documented to
exhibit evidence of late Quaternary displacement, including scarps, offset alluvial deposits, and linear
basin-margin geomorphology (Wong et al. 1995). Although recurrence intervals on individual faults may be
long, seismic hazard remains important because large-magnitude earthquakes can occur on slowly slipping
intraplate normal faults. Ground shaking hazards are generally greater near major basin-bounding faults
and in areas underlain by unconsolidated basin-fill sediments that may amplify seismic waves.

Overall, the seismotectonic setting of the Project reflects the transition from relatively stable cratonic crust
in west Texas to actively extending continental crust in southern New Mexico and Arizona. Contemporary
seismicity is controlled by a combination of inherited basement structures, ongoing Basin and Range and
Rio Grande rift extension, localized Quaternary fault activity, and anthropogenic influences associated with
energy development.

7.1.3            Ground Shaking Hazard
7.1.3.1          PROBABILISTIC GROUND MOTION ESTIMATES
Ground shaking was characterized along the Project using the USGS 2023 National Seismic Hazard Model
(NSHM) for the conterminous United States (Petersen et al. 2024), accessed through the USGS Earthquake
Hazard Toolbox. PGA values were obtained along the Project for a 2,475-year return period (2 percent
probability of exceedance in 50 years) and for two site conditions: Vs30 (defined as the time-averaged
shear wave velocity in the upper 30 meters) of 760 meters per second (m/s) and 260 m/s, representing
the Site Class B/C boundary and D, respectively.

No federal or state regulation prescribes a seismic hazard level for the design of buried natural gas
transmission pipelines. Federal pipeline safety regulations require operators to identify seismicity, geology,
and soil stability as threats for covered segments under the gas transmission integrity management
provisions of 49 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) §192.917, following the data-gathering approach of
American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME 2004) B31.8S, but they establish no design ground
motion or return period. Arizona, New Mexico, and Texas each adopt 49 CFR Part 192 by reference and
add no seismic-specific design standard for gas pipelines. Industry guidance for buried pipelines provides
a performance-based methodology in which the hazard level is selected by the owner rather than prescribed
(PRCI, 2017).

In the absence of a pipeline-specific criterion, ground shaking was characterized at a return period of
approximately 2,475 years, corresponding to a 2 percent probability of exceedance in 50 years. This is the
maximum considered earthquake hazard level associated with building design under American Society of
Civil Engineers (ASCE) 7 as adopted by the International Building Code, and it is a widely applied and
defensible basis for characterizing seismic hazard for critical infrastructure. It is also consistent with the
hazard basis applicable to aboveground piping at the proposed compressor stations, which is designed to
ASCE 7 ground motions in accordance with ASME B31E. Adopting this level provides a single basis for
characterizing ground shaking along the buried mainline and at the aboveground facilities.

Contributing seismic sources along the Project are predominantly shallow crustal earthquakes. The NSHM
represents these sources in two ways: as discrete fault sources, where mapped Quaternary faults with
characterized geometry and slip rate are modeled explicitly, and as gridded (background) seismicity, which
accounts for earthquakes in areas that lack an identifiable fault expression. Along the eastern portion of
the Project, where seismicity is diffuse and largely lacks surface fault expression, the hazard is dominated
by gridded sources. Farther west, across the Rio Grande rift and Basin and Range provinces, mapped
Quaternary normal faults contribute a progressively larger share of the hazard.

The 2023 NSHM is developed from earthquake catalogs that exclude induced earthquakes (Petersen et al.
2024). As discussed in Section 7.1.2, much of the recorded seismicity within 62 miles of the eastern portion
of the Project is interpreted to be induced by wastewater injection associated with hydrocarbon production.
Ground motions from the 2023 NSHM therefore do not account for these sources, and the values
presented in Table 7-2 below may not represent ground shaking hazard along the Permian Basin portion
of the Project for as long as injection-related seismicity continues at current rates. A deterministic seismic
hazard analysis was therefore performed to estimate PGA from representative induced seismicity scenarios
and presented in the subsequent section.

The ground motions along the Project are also influenced by local near-surface geologic conditions. Thick
unconsolidated alluvial deposits within structural basins may amplify ground motion during earthquakes,
whereas mountainous bedrock areas generally present lower amplification potential. Site class, defined by
Vs30, is typically used to account for those conditions. Figures 2b and 2c and Table 7-2 present PGA values
for two site conditions: Site Class D (stiff soil), modeled at Vs30 of 260 m/s, and the Site Class B/C
boundary (rock or very dense soil), modeled at Vs30 of 760 m/s. Site Class D values are greater than the
corresponding B/C values because of soil amplification.

Site Class D was selected as the primary basis for characterizing ground shaking. The Project traverses
predominantly basin-fill and alluvial deposits, including the sediment-filled basins described in Section 4.1,
and shear wave velocity measurements were not obtained for this evaluation. Site Class D is representative
of these deposits and is appropriate for a route-wide screening-level characterization. Where the Project is
underlain by shallow bedrock, site conditions are stiffer and ground motions would be lower, so the Site
Class B/C values are more representative of those reaches. Together the two site conditions bracket the
range of ground shaking expected along the Project.

7.1.3.2          DETERMINISTIC INDUCED SEISMICITY SCENARIO
As discussed in Section 7.1.3.1, the 2023 NSHM excludes induced earthquakes and therefore does not
account for the injection-related seismicity that dominates the recorded catalog along the eastern portion
of the Project. To characterize ground shaking from these sources, a deterministic seismic hazard analysis
was performed using scenario earthquakes selected from the historical catalog described in Section 7.1.2.
Three scenarios intended to bracket the range of ground shaking that could be produced by a recurrence
of the observed seismicity were selected: the largest recorded earthquake within approximately 62 miles
of the Project (Mw 5.4 at a rupture distance of 10.9 miles); the closest recorded earthquake of engineering
significance, which is the second largest event and occurs at a shorter distance (Mw 5.0 at a rupture
distance of 7.6 miles); and the closest recorded earthquake of any magnitude in the catalog (Mw 3.1 at a
rupture distance of 3.1 miles assuming the earthquake focal depth is about 3.0 miles).

Ground motions for the Mw 5.4 and Mw 5.0 scenarios were estimated using the NGA-West2 ground motion
models, applying four of the five models with equal weighting and excluding the Idriss (2014) model. The
four models include Abrahamson et al. (2014), Boore et al. (2014), Campbell and Bozorgnia (2014), and
Chiou and Youngs (2014). Ground motions for the Mw 3.1 scenario were estimated using the Atkinson
(2015) model, which was developed for small to moderate magnitude earthquakes at short rupture
distances and is better suited to that scenario than the NGA-West2 models. Site conditions were taken to
be consistent with those used for the probabilistic evaluation presented in Section 7.1.3.1. Results are
summarized in Table 7-3.

The deterministic scenarios yield estimated PGA values of up to 0.14 g, which is comparable to the
maximum Site Class D value obtained from the probabilistic evaluation presented in Section 7.1.3.1.

7.1.3.3          PIPELINE RESPONSE TO GROUND SHAKING
Investigations by Honegger (1999a) on the source of damage to a 1930s vintage oxyacetylene pipeline
damaged in the 1994 Northridge earthquake concluded that the potential for transmission pipeline
damage from ground shaking (propagation seismic waves) is limited to buried pipelines with extremely poor
quality girth welds or severe corrosion defects and very high levels of seismic ground motion (peak ground
velocities greater than 3 feet/second).

The only documented case of damage to a continuous steel pipeline believed to have been caused by
earthquake wave propagation is a water pipeline damaged in the 1985 Michoacán earthquake (O'Rourke
and Ayala 1989). The 42-inch pipeline was constructed in 1970 with API 5L Grade X42 steel with a wall
thickness of 0.313 inches (pipe diameter and wall thickness [D/t] ratio of 134). The operating pressure for
the water pipeline was less than 60 psi. There is no information on the type of joints used for the water
pipeline but typical water pipeline practice in North America is to construct steel pipelines using welded slip
joints (i.e., pipe with one end formed into a bell).

While wave propagation was highly suspected as the cause of the pipeline damage, O’Rourke and Ayala
could not conclusively state that the pipeline damage was the result of wave propagation. Their assumption
that damage was due to wave propagation was based upon several factors:

■ The pipeline was located in deep, unconsolidated, weak lakebed deposits, unique to a specific region
    near Mexico City.
■ The ground shaking affecting the pipeline was likely from Rayleigh waves based on the observation
    that the lakebed deposits experienced relatively high peak ground velocities following the decay of
    initial higher-frequency ground motions at adjacent firm ground locations.
■ The earthquake produced a relatively long record of sustained sinusoidal variation in ground velocity
    with peak velocities in the range of 1.0 to 1.1 feet/second.
■ No evidence of permanent ground displacement was observed near the locations of pipeline damage.

The operating pressure, D/t ratio, and field weld quality control for water pipelines are generally not typical
of standard design and construction practices used for oil and gas pipelines over the past 50 years.
Furthermore, the geologic conditions required to generate significant wave propagation strains are unique
to the deep lakebed deposits near Mexico City. These factors likely explain the absence of documented
cases in which wave propagation has caused significant distortion of welded steel pipelines design and
constructed in accordance with practices typical of those used in natural gas and liquid hydrocarbon
pipelines.

Some Japanese researchers (Horikawa et al. 2012; Shinkai et al. 2012) have hypothesized that upheaval
buckling of small-diameter pipelines was caused by seismic wave propagation. This hypothesis is based
upon an observation of upheaval buckling following the M 6.6 2007 Niigata Chuetsu earthquake. In the
references cited, no information is provided on the basis for assuming the large strains necessary to
produce upheaval buckling were the result of wave propagation. Given the moderate magnitude of the
earthquake (M 6.6), the shallow depth, the earthquake’s epicenter (25 km offshore), and the relatively
good soil conditions at the location of pipeline damage, the inference that ground shaking caused the
upheaval buckling is highly questionable.

Research on localized ground strains associated with earthquake ground shaking (e.g., Ancheta et al. 2011;
Gupta 2004; Paolucci and Smerzini 2008; Scandella et al. 2008) has utilized the traditional approach for
accounting for the portion of ground strain related to wave propagation developed by Newmark (1967).
Two other factors that are considered to have an influence on ground strains are the incoherency and
amplification of body waves. These effects have been investigated with respect to developing methods to
estimate ground strains that might occur at a local area (e.g., less than 100 by 100 feet per Gupta 2004).
Little, if any, research has been conducted to determine the effects of coherency and amplification on the
development of ground strain along a long linear structure such as a buried pipeline. However, the results
of research by Ancheta et al. (2008) supports a conclusion that the influence of incoherence rapidly
diminishes when the distance between two points on the ground surface used to determine ground strain
exceeds a few tens of meters. Since the length of pipeline that must be exposed to a coherent ground strain
pattern in order to develop significant pipeline strain is much greater than a few tens of meters, coherency
and amplification effects are not considered relevant to the determination of pipeline strain.

In addition to the lack of evidence that ground shaking is a significant hazard to buried steel pipelines,
experience in evaluating the effects of wave propagation on pipeline projects throughout the world has
consistently shown the effects to be negligible.

However, there are some cases that may merit special consideration. These primarily involve pipelines with
compromised pipe strength related to significant weld flaws, corrosion defects, and other pipe connections
with axial strength much less than the pipe body such as compression couplings, bell and spigot joints, or
insulation joints. These factors are not relevant to the proposed pipeline installation.

A recent UCLA research project utilizing state-of-the art earthquake ground motion simulations for
earthquakes with magnitude 6.5, 7.0, and 7.5 provides abundant evidence that seismic wave propagation
is not a significant hazard to buried energy pipelines (Peng et al. 2025). The findings from the UCLA
research project can best be summarized by Figure 7-1 showing the relationship between peak ground
velocity and maximum pipe strain. The approximate peak ground velocity consistent with the level of ground
shaking previously discussed, indicated in Figure 7-1, corresponds to a maximum axial strain of less than
0.01 percent, 50 times less than the nominal pipeline steel yield strain.

7.1.4             Fault Rupture
7.1.4.1           GENERAL
Fault rupture can occur entirely within the subsurface or may progress to the surface along a particular
fault trace. The nature of movement at the surface depends on whether the fault movement is normal
(extension), reverse or thrusting (compressional), strike slip (horizontal shearing), or a combination of these
fault movement types. Surface rupture associated with a large earthquake can result in rapid differential
ground movement on the order of feet to tens of feet, with the nature of that movement determined by the
fault type and earthquake magnitude. In general, surface fault rupture across a pipeline can cause
differential ground displacements across the pipe.

In the United States, the USGS categorizes potential seismic faults based on the age of the most recent
surface rupture and/or deformation:

■ Historical fault – a fault that has moved within the past 150 years,
■ Holocene - a fault that has moved within the past 11,000 years,
■ Latest Quaternary fault – a fault that has moved within the past 15,000 years,
■ Late Quaternary fault – a fault that has moved in the past 130,000 years,
■ Middle and Late Quaternary fault – a fault that has moved in the past 750,000 years, and
■ Undifferentiated Quaternary fault – a fault that has moved in the past 1,600,000 years.


  File No. 18782-065-00
 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                                       Page 23




For seismically active regions near tectonic plate boundaries, such as the western United States, faults of
Latest Quaternary and younger age are typically considered to be active and capable of generating large
(Mw 6+) earthquakes, with associated surface fault rupture and a recurrence interval of hundreds to
several thousand years. Late Quaternary faults are typically considered potentially active but with a lower
potential to generate a large (Mw 6+) earthquake with associated surface rupture within a typical project
lifetime.
