7.1.5            Liquefaction and Liquefaction-Induced Hazards
7.1.5.1          GENERAL
Liquefaction is the process by which saturated, loose, cohesionless materials (gravel, sand, sandy silt, low
plasticity silt) lose their shear strength due to increased pore water pressures that occur during seismic
shaking. Liquefaction is generally associated with thick deposits of saturated, loose to medium dense
granular alluvium, typically in low lying alluvial plains with high groundwater conditions that are subject to



 File No. 18782-065-00
 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                               Page 25




relatively strong ground motions. Loose clean sand deposits saturated by a high groundwater table are
most susceptible.

This loss of soil strength can result in buoyant displacement of buried structures, ground settlement, and
ground lateral displacement (spreading). Buoyant displacement occurs because a buried pipeline is less
dense than the surrounding liquefied soil and can float upward. Flotation is most likely for large diameter
gas pipelines with shallow cover and the resulting upward displacement can bend the pipe and expose it
at the ground surface. We understand that buoyancy design for the pipeline is typically completed,
assuming no resisting contribution from the shear strength of the soil, which is equivalent to assuming fully
liquefied soil conditions. This liquefaction-induced hazard is therefore already accounted for in the pipeline
design and is not discussed further below.

Ground settlement occurs as excess pore water pressures dissipate following shaking and liquefied soil
reconsolidates. Broad, uniform settlement is generally well accommodated by continuously welded steel
pipe, whereas differential settlement across short distances imposes bending on the pipe. The amount of
ground settlement is proportional to the cumulative thickness of the liquefied soil layers, the density of the
liquefied layers, as measure by standard blow counts, and the factor of safety against liquefaction. The
most severe liquefaction hazards typically exhibit volumetric strains in the range of 3±0.5 percent. For a
site with a 50-feet thickness of liquefiable soil, this translates to 18±3 inches. This amount of displacement
occurs over a broad distance (a few hundred feet). However, displacements of this magnitude at locations
where the pipeline is connected to equipment supported on deep foundations (e.g., piles) can lead to
localized high bending in the pipeline.

Lateral spreading involves horizontal displacement of surficial blocks of non-liquefied soil as the underlying
soil layer liquefies, loses strength, and flows under the influence of gravity until pore pressures can drain.
It generally develops where sloping ground is present or near a free face, such as along the banks of rivers,
sloughs, canals, or lakes, and because it requires a slope, the depth of movement usually is limited to the
slope toe or channel bottom elevation. Displacements typically range from inches to several feet and
concentrate at the head and toe of the spread zone, imposing tensile and compressive strain on a pipeline
crossing those margins. If liquefaction were to occur within loose to medium dense saturated sand
deposits, there would be a high potential for lateral spreading to occur along slopes or near a free face.

Lateral spreading has potential to damage a buried pipeline because the permanent ground deformation
can impose localized strain on the pipe. Lateral spreading requires sloping ground or a nearby free face, so
it is screened based on topography as well as soil conditions. Ground settlement is generally distributed
over a longer distance and is accommodated by continuously welded steel pipe, although differential
settlement across short distances can impose bending on the pipe. The following subsections present our
evaluation of liquefaction potential and, where liquefaction is possible, the resulting potential risk of
liquefaction-induced hazards.

7.1.5.2          LIQUEFACTION ANALYSIS METHODOLOGY
The liquefaction analysis consisted of a desktop study along the mainline and laterals to identify areas that
are potentially susceptible to seismically induced liquefaction and associated hazards. We evaluated
liquefaction potential and associated hazards using the methodology presented in the FEMA Hazus
Earthquake Model Technical Manual (FEMA 2024).




 File No. 18782-065-00
 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                                 Page 26




There are three conditions necessary to cause liquefaction: (1) sufficient earthquake duration, magnitude
and PGA; (2) the presence of non-cohesive soil; and (3) shallow groundwater saturating the soils.
The following paragraphs discuss our liquefaction risk assessment relative to these three conditions, and
address potential of liquefaction-induced hazards to the Project.

For a given site, the Hazus methodology first assigns a liquefaction susceptibility category using geologic
map information, including the type of deposit and geologic age, and following the liquefaction susceptibility
table presented by Youd and Perkins (1978). The method then estimates the probability of liquefaction as
a function of the liquefaction susceptibility category, the peak ground acceleration at the site, and
correction factors for earthquake magnitude and depth to groundwater.

Because lateral spreading is associated with liquefaction of soils, we evaluated lateral spreading using the
same Hazus framework. Expected permanent ground displacement is estimated from the ratio of the site
PGA to a threshold acceleration for the susceptibility category, scaled by a magnitude correction factor.
Threshold accelerations are 0.09 g for the “very high” category and 0.12 g for the “high” category.

The Hazus methodology estimates liquefaction-induced ground settlement by assigning a characteristic
settlement amount to each susceptibility category and multiplying that amount by the probability of
liquefaction calculated for the site. Expected settlement therefore depends on the susceptibility category
and the ground motion.

7.1.5.3          POTENTIAL OF LIQUEFACTION AND LIQUEFACTION-INDUCED HAZARDS
The liquefaction susceptibility relationship presented by Youd and Perkins (1978) in the Hazus methodology
assigns each combination of the type of deposit and geologic age to one of six susceptibility categories:
very high, high, moderate, low, very low and none. Only one combination of the type of deposit and geologic
age was assigned within the very high susceptibility category, which is deposits within a river channel in the
past 500 years.

The Project crosses several river channels. The most significant threat from liquefaction at river and stream
crossings is lateral spread displacement at the banks. Based upon historical observations, lateral spread
displacement at riverbanks can extend as much as 1,000 feet from the riverbank.

We anticipate these locations may be assigned to the “very high” susceptibility category. The Project,
however, will be installed beneath major river crossings by means of horizontal directional drilling methods
(HDD) or other trenchless crossing methods at depths of typically 50 to 100 feet, well below the depth at
which liquefaction of channel deposits would affect the pipeline. The potential for liquefaction-induced
damage at the areas classified as very high susceptibility category is therefore considered low. Site-specific
subsurface exploration and design will be completed for the HDD crossings and will further confirm/address
liquefaction potential in these areas. We hence excluded river channel crossings from subsequent
quantitative probability of liquefaction analysis.

The most common deposits along the remainder of the Project are alluvial fan and plain deposits and
lacustrine and playa deposits. Where these deposits are of modern age, defined by Youd and Perkins
(1978) as less than 500 years, they are categorized as “moderate” and “high” susceptibility, respectively.
For the probability of liquefaction analysis, we conservatively assigned a “high” susceptibility category to all
mapped geologic units along the Project other than the river channel crossings discussed above.

7.1.6            Seismically Induced Landslides and Rockfalls
Strong ground shaking associated with earthquakes can cause landslides and rockfalls, even at long
distances from the source. Keefer (1984) notes that an Mw 7.3 earthquake, for example, could result in
landslides to about 60 miles away from the earthquake source, and rockfalls to a maximum of 90 miles
from the source. For an Mw 6.6 event, lateral spreads and flows could occur up to about 55 miles from the
source. Keefer also notes that rockfalls associated with earthquakes only occurred on slopes steeper than

40 degrees (~84 percent), and that landslides in sedimentary rock occurred on slopes greater than
15 degrees (~27 percent).

The slope classes summarized in Section 3.2 were defined for pipeline constructability rather than for
landslide susceptibility, so they do not align directly with the slope thresholds reported by Keefer (1984).
Over 97 percent of the mainline and over 99 percent of the laterals fall within the gentle slope class of less
than 33 percent, which includes some terrain marginally steeper than the approximately 27 percent
gradient on which Keefer observed landslides in sedimentary rock. The available slope data does not
resolve the length of the mainline and laterals that fall between 27 and 33 percent. Slopes steeper than
33 percent occur as short, localized segments adjacent to streams, rivers, and canyon walls, and they
account for about 2 percent of the mainline and less than 1 percent of the laterals. Very steep slopes,
steeper than 67 percent, account for about 0.1 percent of the mainline and laterals, so terrain approaching
the approximately 84 percent gradient that Keefer associates with earthquake induced rockfalls is rare
along the route. Considering the limited extent of these steeper slopes and the relatively low expected PGA
values, we consider the probability of seismically induced landslides and rockfalls along the Project to be
low.

7.1.7            Seismic Hazards Conclusions
As described in Section 7.1.3, ground shaking is not considered a credible seismic hazard for the Project.

As described in Section 7.1.4, the Project crosses one Latest Quaternary normal fault, the East Franklin
Mountains fault, that is considered by the USGS to be active. The Project crosses two mapped strands of
this fault. McCalpin et al. (2021) report evidence of five faulting events at a study site along the East
Franklin Mountains fault over the past 44,000 years, the last three exhibiting vertical displacement of
approximately 10 to 13 feet. This study site is approximately 5.25 miles south of the mainline fault crossing.
While the observations from one site do not necessarily translate to other locations along the fault, these
findings indicate a potential for significant fault displacement if an earthquake were to occur on the East
Franklin Mountains fault.

As described in Section 7.1.5, the analysis indicates that the risk of liquefaction and liquefaction-induced
hazards is low along the Project. Site-specific surface and subsurface data are currently being collected at
discrete locations along the Project including HDD crossings and aboveground facilities. GeoEngineers will
review the subsurface data as it becomes available. If liquefiable soils are identified, GeoEngineers will
address those areas in the final FERC submittal, where mitigation will be described and implemented during
final design if necessary.

As described in Section 7.1.6, the potential for seismically induced landslides and rockfalls is low along the
mainline and laterals, based on the limited extent of steep slopes along the route and the relatively low
anticipated ground motions.

7.2        KARST
Karst terrain can pose a hazard to pipeline infrastructure through ground subsidence, sinkhole collapse,
erosion, and loss of pipeline support. The term “karst” generally refers to terrain developed in soluble
bedrock and characterized by landforms such as sinkholes, sinking streams, springs, caves, and
subsurface voids (Ford and Williams 2007). Karst-related ground disturbance may also develop where
dissolution occurs at depth and resulting voids propagate upward to the ground surface. Similar surface


 File No. 18782-065-00
 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                             Page 29




features, commonly referred to as pseudokarst, may develop through piping or internal erosion within
sedimentary or volcanic rocks.

The distribution of mature surface karst in the United States is primarily dependent on two factors: soluble
rocks at or near the surface, and precipitation above approximately 30 inches per year (Weary and Doctor
2014). In humid regions of the United States, prominent karst features typically develop in carbonate rocks,
including limestone and dolomite. In arid and semi-arid regions, lower precipitation generally limits the
dissolution of carbonate rocks, and the most prominent karst features commonly occur in more soluble
evaporite deposits that exist at or near the surface in those environments (Weary and Doctor 2014). The
Project is located primarily in areas that receive an average rainfall of about 10 to 15 inches per year
(National Centers for Environmental Information [NCEI 2026]) and is thus considered primarily a semi-arid
region. As such, karst is expected to occur in the Project area where evaporite rocks (anhydrite, gypsum,
salt) are exposed at or near the surface.

7.2.1            Karst Hazard Evaluation
7.2.1.1          DESKTOP EVALUATION
A desktop study was performed of the following sources to evaluate potential karst areas along the Project.
A site reconnaissance was then completed to ground-truth the desktop interpretations and to further
assess the risk to the Project.

The following were reviewed to evaluate potential karst topography along the Project:

■ LiDAR hillshade model developed for the Project using publicly available LiDAR data obtained from the
    USGS 3DEP program (USGS 2026d);
■ Historical aerial imagery: photo-record from 1990 to 2026 viewed on Google Earth™ software;
■ USGS topographic maps; and
■ Various scientific publications as referenced.

The USGS digital map compilation and database of Karst in the United States (Weary and Doctor 2014)
was also reviewed. This mapping compiles digital maps delineating areas of the United States having karst
or the potential for development of karst and pseudokarst by showing areas underlain by soluble rocks
(both carbonate and evaporites) or areas underlain by sedimentary rocks known to contain piping or other
pseudokarst features. The USGS Karst Mapping for the Conterminous United States is shown with respect
to the Project in Figure 3. The USGS mapping indicates that the pipeline crosses:

■ Carbonate rocks at or near the surface in a dry climate,

7.3        EARTH FISSURES
7.3.1            Earth Fissures Evaluation
Earth fissures occur in several arid basins of central and southeastern Arizona. These features are ground
cracks that develop primarily in response to differential land subsidence associated with long-term
groundwater withdrawal. Earth fissures are an anthropogenic geologic hazard that can threaten people,
livestock, property, and infrastructure, including roads, pipelines, canals, and utilities.

Earth fissures range from discontinuous hairline fractures to large, open ground cracks. Documented
fissures may extend for as much as approximately 2 miles, reach widths of approximately 15 to 25 feet,
and extend to depths of as much as approximately 90 feet. Intense runoff during monsoon storms can
enter existing fissures and rapidly enlarge them through erosion, piping, and collapse of soil bridges. As a
result, fissures that initially appear narrow or discontinuous at the ground surface may develop into larger
openings that pose hazards to people, livestock, and infrastructure (Arizona Geological Survey 2026b).

A desktop study was performed of the following sources to evaluate potential earth fissures along the

further assess the risk to the Project from earth fissures.

      obtained from the USGS 3DEP program (USGS 2026d);
■ Historical aerial imagery: photo-record from 1990 to 2026 viewed on Google Earth™ software;
■ USGS topographic maps; and
■ Various scientific publications as cited herein.

Based on these sources, known and interpreted earth-fissure features were mapped within the study

As discussed above, six areas with earth fissure development were identified. Specific traces were
delineated when near the mainline or lateral pipeline centerlines. Although earth fissure propagation has

Petroleum Institute (API) recommended practice (RP) 1117 (API 2008). The analysis indicates the mainline

the pipeline be aligned at an acute angle relative to a fissure that develops across the pipeline, the safe
span distance could be exceeded. We expect that annual inspections can identify fissure propagation and

7.4        VOLCANIC HAZARDS
7.4.1            Volcanic Hazards Evaluation
Volcanic hazards along the Project were evaluated based on a review of regional volcanic features (USGS
2026g) and published geologic mapping by the USGS for New Mexico (Mullineaux 1978). Volcanic hazards
occur in areas subject to lahars, tephra fall, lava flows, and pyroclastic flows resulting from volcanic activity
originating from local volcanoes. All of these hazards have the potential to bury or interfere with above-
ground pipeline facilities. The degree of risk from these hazards depends on the proximity of the volcanic
vent to the Project, wind direction and velocity during the eruption and the topography between the vent
and the Project.

One volcanic vent (VV-1) was identified within the study corridor (see Sheet 51 of the Geologic Hazards and
Conditions Maps in Appendix B). VV-1 is located approximately 0.25 miles south of the mainline at
approximate MP 247.3 and is part of the Potrillo Volcanic Field which is located on the Rio Grande Rift in
southern New Mexico. The Potrillo Volcanic Field contains more than 150 cinder cones and is located about
22 miles southwest of Las Cruces, New Mexico, covering roughly 1,800 square miles. The field was active
during the Quaternary, and no Holocene eruptive activity has been documented (Wood and Kienle 1990).
Given the absence of documented Holocene activity, volcanic hazards are not anticipated to pose a risk to
the Project during its operational life.

The purpose of the Phase 1 Study is to screen a large crossing inventory, categorize crossings by their risk
of erosion-related pipeline exposure, and prioritize a subset for focused Phase 2 numerical scour and
channel-stability evaluation.

The approach utilizes a quantitative component generally following the published logistic regression
equations presented by Homan (2024). Drainage area, sinuosity, boundary shear stress at the 10-year
flow, and width-to-depth ratio at the 10-year flow are entered directly into the equation to calculate a
regression-based probability of active erosion.

Direct geomorphic evidence and pipeline vulnerability are evaluated separately from the regression
probability. This separation preserves transparency and avoids treating the source equation as a complete
predictor of pipeline exposure. Clear evidence of headcutting, incision, bank erosion, or potential avulsion,
observed in the aerial imagery or LiDAR hillshade model may elevate a crossing regardless of its regression
probability.

8.0 Impacts and Mitigation
8.1        SEISMIC HAZARDS
The seismic-hazards evaluation identified potential surface rupture along the East Franklin Mountains fault
as the only seismic hazard that poses a risk to the mainline and laterals. Geotechnical and geological
risks related to the aboveground facilities will be considered in forthcoming site-specific geotechnical
evaluations.

Buried pipelines accommodate fault displacement by bending and elongating to match the imposed ground
displacement pattern. For normal faults, the ground on one side of the fault trace would move downward
relative to the other during a fault rupture event. This is generally the most benign type of fault displacement
for a buried steel pipeline as the maximum soil forces acting to bend the pipeline are limited to the force
necessary to pull the pipeline upward out of the ground, which are typically 15 percent to 20 percent of the
horizontal soil forces for common depths of cover.

In evaluating pipeline response, longitudinal strains beyond the yield strain can be acceptable provided the
loading condition on the pipeline limits the pipeline displacement to the displacement of the surrounding
soil. Vertical displacements much greater than the depth of soil cover over the pipeline will result in a free
span condition where yielding in bending at the upthrown side of the fault could lead to a plastic hinge with
a potential for pipeline rupture. For the free-span condition, the allowable strain in the pipeline is limited to
the yield strain of the pipe steel.

The axial force in the pipeline generated by normal fault displacement can be substantial and extend
hundreds of feet from the point of surface rupture. High axial forces in the pipeline could lead to
concentration of pipeline strains at the location of bends in the pipeline. Locations where this might occur
includes a horizontal bend approximately 1,100 feet from the west fault trace in the USGS fault database.

The impact of permanent ground displacement on buried pipelines can be reduced in several ways:

■ Increasing the pipe wall thickness provides two benefits. First, the strength of the pipeline is increased.
      largely in proportion to the increase in wall thickness. Increasing the pipe wall thickness also leads to
      increased strain capacity by minimizing the influence of circumferential flaws in girth welds. It is noted
      that increasing the strength of the pipe is generally not a preferred mitigation strategy since this can
      reduce the potential for girth welds that are not stronger than the pipe, a fundamental requirement for
      strain-based design.
■ Axial and vertical uplift soil loads can be decreased by importing fine granular soil for backfill and
      minimizing the depth of burial and degree of backfill compaction.
■ Where it is not practicable to import backfill material, axial soil loads can be reduced by wrapping the
      pipeline in two layers of geotextile fabric.
■ Horizontal soil loads can be reduced by over-excavating the pipe trench in a trapezoidal shape,
      minimizing the depth of soil cover, backfilling the trench with imported granular soil and minimizing soil
      compaction.
■ The potential for strain concentration at bends can be reduced by increasing the pipe bend radius (e.g.,
      replacing long radius elbows with induction bends or replacing induction bends with field bends).


 File No. 18782-065-00
 Gulf Interstate Engineering Company | September 21, 2026                                                Page 39




■ The allowable strain capacity of the pipeline can be increased by imposing more stringent girth weld
      procedures, weld inspection methods, and flaw acceptance criteria. This is most feasible for situations
      such as fault crossings where a limited number of welds are subject to the more stringent measures.
■ For locations where the consequences of associated with a very low likelihood of pipeline rupture can
      be accepted, operational mitigation measure may be sufficient. In many instances, operational
      mitigation measures are the only practicable alternative for the same reasons associated with pipeline
      realignment. These measures typically include one or more of the following:
          Reduce the spacing of line-break valves to minimize the length of time for gas release. The location
           of these valves should be sufficiently far from the fault rupture zone to not be impacted by axial
           forces in the pipeline generated by fault displacement.

Several of the physical mitigation measures described above are either already incorporated into the
proposed pipeline design or are not considered sufficiently beneficial or practicable for this crossing. The
proposed pipeline has a relatively heavy wall thickness, which provides increased strength and strain
capacity. Measures involving specialized backfill, reduced compaction, trench over-excavation, or geotextile
wrapping require reasonably accurate identification of the fault rupture location to be effective. Given the
uncertainty in the location and width of the potential surface-rupture zone, accurately defining the fault
location could require extensive subsurface investigation, trenching, and associated ground disturbance in
order to define the length of pipeline requiring special mitigation measures and the most effective
mitigation measures. In addition, several nearby road crossings require adequately compacted backfill,
which limits the practicability of maintaining low-compaction backfill through portions of the fault-crossing
area. FEA modeling also indicates that specialized backfill provides relatively modest improvement in
pipeline response compared with the native granular soils expected along the Project.

More importantly, there is low confidence that these measures would appreciably reduce the potential for
pipeline rupture during a design-level fault displacement. Accordingly, the mitigation strategy does not rely
on the pipeline remaining intact during such an event. Instead, the preferred approach is to reduce the
consequences of a potential rupture through operational mitigation measures, including appropriate line-
break valve placement, ground-disturbance monitoring where practicable, and enhanced welding,
inspection, and flaw-acceptance requirements through the fault-crossing area. With the implementation of
these mitigation measures, Transwestern anticipates that Project risks associated with seismic hazards
will be reduced to less than significant levels.

■ If voids extending below the planned maximum excavation depth below ground surface are
      encountered elsewhere on the Project during construction, they should be evaluated on a case-by-case
      basis by an SME experienced with karst prior to attempting over-excavation and repair.

8.3        VOLCANIC HAZARDS
The potential threat of volcanic hazards such as lahars, tephra fall, lava flows, and pyroclastic flows from
the Potrillo Volcanic Field is not a concern because no Holocene eruptive activity has been documented in
the volcanic field. Therefore, there are no recommended mitigation measures, and Transwestern
anticipates that Project risks associated with volcanic hazards will not be significant.

8.4        LANDSLIDES AND SLOPE STABILITY
No existing landslides were identified within the study corridor that require avoidance or mitigation.
However, the Project crosses locally steep slopes in areas mapped as higher risk by the U.S. Landslide
Susceptibility Map. Construction could affect slope stability through: (1) deep excavation where the pipeline
traverses slopes in a side-slope orientation; and (2) the collection and conveyance of surface or near-
surface water along the right-of-way or within the trench toward potentially unstable slopes.

As described in Section 3.2, approximately 97 percent of the route avoids steep terrain. To reduce
construction-related landslide hazards, the mainline and lateral pipelines are routed to avoid traversing

steep to very steep slopes with an orientation parallel or oblique to contour (side slope) where practicable.
Construction oriented parallel or oblique to contour will require deep excavations to establish the
construction corridor. Less than 1 cumulative mile of the mainline and laterals traverses steep to very steep
slopes in the side-slope orientation.

To reduce the risk of construction-related adverse impacts to slope stability, the following mitigation
measures will be implemented during the design and construction phases of the Project.

■ Geotechnical specifications will be developed and implemented for temporary and permanent fill
      placement on all slopes with a gradient of 2H:1V or steeper.
■ Subsurface drainage will be provided as necessary to maintain stability of constructed slopes in steep
      terrain.
■ Surface water runoff will be effectively managed by placing water bars at regular intervals based on the
      slope gradient in accordance with the Project erosion and sediment control plans.
■ Trench plugs and drains (where appropriate) will be installed in the pipe ditch at regular intervals based
      on the slope gradient in accordance with the erosion and sediment control plans.

With the implementation of these mitigation measures, Transwestern anticipates that Project risks
associated with landslides and slope stability will be reduced to less than significant levels.

8.5        STREAM SCOUR, MIGRATION, AND FLOODING
The Phase 1 and Phase 2 (to be completed) evaluation described in Appendix C-1 will be used to establish
a pipeline burial depth to reduce the risk of future pipeline exposure resulting from scour, migration, and
flooding processes at surveyed waterbody crossings. Increased burial depth will be the preferred mitigation
where it is technically feasible and provides adequate protection against the calculated scour and
degradation hazard.

Where the identified hazard cannot be reasonably mitigated through increased burial depth, additional
measures will be evaluated and incorporated into the final design plans. These may include grade control,
channel stabilization, armoring, bank protection, trenchless installation, alignment modification,
monitoring, or other site-specific measures.

8.6        BLASTING
8.6.1            Blasting Impacts Evaluation
Mitigation measures will be incorporated into a blasting program to minimize adverse impacts to the
environment and nearby water sources, structures, pipelines and utilities. Blasting will be conducted in
accordance with all federal, state, and local regulations and Transwestern’s Blasting Plan, which is
presented in Resource Report 1, Appendix 1H under separate cover. The following sections describe the
potential blasting impacts and the related mitigation measures.

8.6.1.1          WATER WELLS
In general, vibration effects would be expected to be limited to the immediate proximity of the blasting. A
common measurement unit for vibration is the peak particle velocity (PPV) of blasting-induced ground
motion in inches/second. Siskind (1999) summarizes information on four blasting studies conducted to
evaluate vibration effects on wells. One study of blasting effects on 24 wells conducted under contract
to the United States Bureau of Mines (USBM) showed, “There were no physical vibration effects on
the wells even as close as 300 feet.” The maximum velocities for this testing ranged from 0.84 to
5.44 inches/second, with four of the five sites exceeding 2 inches/second. In another USBM study
described in Siskind (1999), a well was tested for casing cement bond damage. The study indicated initial
bond losses occurred at a PPV of 4.7 inches/second. A third study in Siskind (1999) indicated that wells
outside the blast pattern were exposed to as much as PPV of 8.7 inches/second at a distance of 31 feet
and no damage occurred; however, the construction details for these wells are not described in the Siskind
(1999) report.

Transwestern will request authorization from landowners to test and document the baseline condition, yield
and water quality of any private wells located within 200 feet of the construction ROW. This testing will
occur before construction starts in the nearby area, and the testing results will be shared with the property
owner, if requested. Similar information will be gathered for any public water wells located within 400 feet
of the construction ROW.

Maximum ground motion velocities of 2 inches/second will be specified at the locations of private and
public water supply wells. In specific cases, relief boreholes may be drilled between the portion of the trench
being blasted and any private or public water wells located within 200 feet of the construction ROW. The
number and location of the relief boreholes will be determined on a site-specific basis.

Any turbidity in wells caused by the blasting vibrations is expected to be temporary and will likely dissipate
after the well is pumped several times. Groundwater quality impacts from blasting agents, if any, are
expected to be temporary and localized because only small amounts of these agents generally will be
needed for trench excavation.

8.6.1.2          SPRINGS
Yields from perennial springs could potentially decrease if blasting vibrations damage the related aquifer.
Any turbidity caused by blasting is expected to be temporary and is likely to dissipate shortly after the
blasting. Water quality impacts to springs from blasting agents, if any, are expected to be temporary and
localized because only small amounts of blasting agents generally will be needed for trenching.

Transwestern will request authorization from landowners to test and document the baseline condition, yield
and water quality of any springs being used as a permitted water supply that are located within 200 feet of
the pipeline construction ROW. This testing will occur before the pipeline construction starts in the nearby
area, and the testing results will be shared with the property owner, if requested. Similar information will
be gathered for any public water supply springs located within 400 feet of the pipeline construction ROW.

No springs were identified during Project surveys.

8.6.1.3          WETLANDS
Blasting could potentially redirect surface water and groundwater flows to and from wetlands. In addition,
turbidity and blasting agent by-products could possibly temporarily degrade surface water and groundwater
quality.

Any turbidity resulting from blasting is expected to be temporary and is expected to dissipate shortly after
blasting. Water quality impacts to wetlands from blasting agents, if any, are expected to be temporary and
localized because only small amounts of blasting agents generally will be needed for trenching.

Surveys identified two wetlands (associated with the Pecos River and Salt Creek in Texas). Both will be
crossed using an HDD; therefore, no wetland impacts are expected.

8.6.1.4          SLOPES
Unstable rock and soil slopes may locally fail as a result of blasting vibrations. A reconnaissance of the
Project in the vicinity of the blasting locations will be completed. The reconnaissance will include measuring
slope inclinations and observing areas adjacent to planned blasting locations for potential indicators of
unstable slopes. Identified slope areas that could be impacted by blasting will be monitored and evaluated
for hazards to people and property during the blasting operations.

8.6.1.5          STRUCTURES
Blasting vibrations and flying debris could potentially damage aboveground structures. If structures are
present in areas where blasting is necessary, Transwestern will request authorization from landowners to
inspect structures located within 200 feet of the construction ROW before and after blasting. Blasting mats
or padding also will be used when blasting in close proximity to structures to limit potential damage from
flying rocks. Maximum ground motion velocities of 2 inches/second will be specified at the locations of
structures (refer to the Blasting Plan in Appendix 1H to Resource Report 1).

As an additional precaution, Transwestern will require the contractor conducting blasting to limit the size
of charges in accordance with the scaled distance factor (SD) guidelines developed by the Office of Surface
Mining Reclamation and Enforcement (OSMRE). The SD is equal to the distance from the blast to an
aboveground structure divided by the square root of the charge (lb/delay). For distances less than 300 feet,
OSMRE states that the SD shall exceed 50. Table 8-1 provides information on the limits of charges as a
function of distance in accordance with OSMRE.

8.6.1.6          ADJACENT PIPELINES AND BURIED UTILITIES
Blasting vibrations could potentially damage adjacent underground pipelines and utilities. In general,
blasting will not be allowed within 10 feet of an existing pipeline or buried utility. In cases where blasting
near an existing utility is necessary, the pipeline or utility owner will be notified in advance of the blasting,
and measures will be taken to minimize the potential for utility damage.

Transwestern can find no regulatory citations for allowing or limiting blasting in the vicinity of other utilities.
The current industry accepted PPV limit for blasting near in-service pipelines is 4 inches per second
adjacent to the pipeline. Whenever blasting occurs near third-party pipelines and other underground
facilities, the more stringent of 4 inches per second or the requirements of the third-party utility operating
company shall be implemented.

8.6.2            Blasting Mitigation
Blasting will be conducted in accordance with all federal, state, and local regulations and Transwestern
Construction Specifications. The blasting plan includes measures to control adverse impacts, including
measures to minimize vibrations and flyrock. In addition, the plan includes appropriate measures for safe
blasting practices near pipelines that satisfy the requirements of the adjacent pipeline operator. Inspectors
will be present to ensure that all specifications are met and to perform pre- and post-blast inspections of
nearby structures and wells. Based on the implementation of these measures, blasting is not expected to
result in significant impacts to the environment.
